This study provides first-time data on the fluctuations of a specific angle, known as $\Psi_n$, and magnitude, known as $v_n$, related to particle flow, which have been determined using a newly developed technique for four-particle correlations. Researchers used ALICE to collect these data in high-energy Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC. Fluctuations in both angle and magnitude are evident across different centralities and become more pronounced in more central collisions and in collisions where the momentum of the particles is higher than 2 GeV/c. These findings, which have been compared to theoretical models such as iEBE-VISHNU, MUSIC, and AMPT, shed new light on the complex and not well understood initial conditions of these collisions. Furthermore, they highlight unique sensitivities to two crucial factors: the viscosity of quark--gluon plasma and the characteristics of the collisions' initial state. Given that these fluctuations tend to increase with the momentum of the particles, there is a need for re-examining existing theoretical models to gain a more precise and unbiased understanding of quark--gluon plasma's properties. Lastly, we have made these results available in the form of tables and figures that can be accessed via the DOIs listed in the paper.

We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after witnessing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization
to locate the pose whose descriptor corresponds to that in the demonstration. NDFs
are efficiently trained without expert input, using a self-supervised 3D
auto-encoder, and exhibit robust performance across 6-DoF rotations and translations.
In experiments, NDFs master tasks from just a handful (5-10) demonstrations,
in both simulation and with a physical robot. Results show our method excels at
generalizing over different object instances and poses, surpassing a comparison
method relying on 2D descriptors. The NDF project is hosted at https://yilundu.github.io/ndf/.

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches. The proposed framework is termed DeepHMap++ and its code has been made publicly available. The proposed project grouping and correspondence learning concepts can also be applied to other object pose estimation techniques. Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using a hybrid algorithm. This new algorithm first determines the degree of separation between different layers and then uses a iterative switching method to solve the equations. We validate our approach by demonstrating that our method corresponds to existing single-layer eigenvector centrality calculations when there is only one layer and show that it provides reliable results on artificially generated networks and real-world data sets. Furthermore, we demonstrate its practical applications in identifying the most influential nodes across multiple layers and in ranking artificial networks. Our approach is also more effective than current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks in maintaining the stability of the results when there are significant changes between different network updates. We conclude that our approach provides a practical and reliable method for calculating the centrality of multi-layered networks and suggest that it can be enhanced further. Our code is available at https://github.com/abdo22/MLEVC.

This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than they do at either low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressures inside the formed cavity play a significant role. In addition, our findings include the shift from the deeper water-entrapment phenomenon to the surface-seal regime, and observations on the partial-seal, rippling-cavity-surface, and secondary pinch-off stages of water-entry interactions. A comprehensive discussion of existing and newly observed phenomena in the surface-seal regime is also presented. Moreover, our research includes an analysis of the effects of increasing velocities on the pressures within the formed cavities, revealing that at mid-range speeds, increased pressures inside the cavities contribute significantly to the dynamics of the water-entry interactions. A notable finding includes the occurrence of the 2-stage pinch-off in the medium-speed range, where the primary pinch-off occurs when the decreasing pressure inside the cavity overcomes the drag force exerted on the sphere, while the secondary pinch-off stage happens when the increasing pressure inside the cavity overcomes the static pressure of the water. Our calculations using first-principles methods reveal that cubanite exhibits unusual orbital selectivity, with electrons occupying certain molecular orbitals while being localized in other atomic ones. This phenomenon is exceptionally rare in 3d transition metal compounds, providing a theoretical basis for the experimentally observed lack of charge disproportionation, anomalous Mössbauer spectra, and ferromagnetic coupling between adjacent iron ions. Moreover, its distinctive feature makes cubanite fascinating for implementing novel 4d or 5d orbital-based functions in superconducting nanocircuits. Additionally, we propose that the cubanite (110)-surface would be suitable for experimental investigation, offering a simpler and more explicit signature of orbital selectivity. Finally, our findings also demonstrate that the unique properties of cubanite can be altered by applying pressure or straining the material, offering a means of exploring pressure-dependent or phonon-assisted orbital selectivity and related phenomena.

A burgeoning field in quantum physics, known as multi-phonon physics, is driving research and development for both fundamental understanding and applications in metrology and communication systems. Quantum acoustic resonators serve as the ideal testing ground for multi-phonon phenomena through a combination of theoretical and experimental studies. The specific system studied consists of a semiconductor quantum dot driven by a laser, coupled to an acoustic cavity, and has exhibited remarkable multi-phonon properties, albeit previously described with a simplistic two-level quantum dot model. However, by accounting for both bright and dark excitons within the quantum dot model, the complexity of this system can be better represented. The inclusion of dark excitons offers a particular advantage, given their inherently low decoherence rates as a result of lacking spontaneous photon emission. Consequently, researchers are now capable of achieving giant Rabi oscillations between a vacuum state and a dark exciton state accompanied by N-phonon bundles by adjusting the laser frequency with precision. Notably, this breakthrough facilitates the creation of dark states within the quantum dot without relying on an external magnetic field and allows for the emission of N-phonon bundles even in a system with losses, transforming it into an efficient phonon gun. The theoretical predictions discussed in this paper have been validated through accurate experimental measurements of both the phonon number distribution and the corresponding Wigner function, which accurately resemble the predicted results. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact in two input ports, and a photon is detected in a specific output channel. We examine the success probabilities associated with detecting these states, as they vary depending on the catalytic device used. Notably, our analysis reveals that states produced by beam splitters and parametric amplifiers exhibit the same characteristics when analyzing the distribution of photons. We thoroughly investigate the unique quantum properties of SPCCSs, including sub-Poisson statistics, anti-bunching effects, and quadrature squeezing. These findings demonstrate that SPCCSs possess abundant non-classical behavior, thereby conferring a quantum advantage for executing various technological tasks. We also explore the potential of SPCCSs in quantum information processing, investigating the accuracy of preparing these states and the associated execution time. Furthermore, we design an optimal catalytic device that maximizes the non-classical property of anti-bunching, thereby ensuring that all generated states possess this particular property. Finally, we discuss the utility of SPCCSs in interference experiments and coherent communication systems, showing that these states can be employed as reference states to validate measurement apparatus and ensure the accuracy of quantum information transmission. We conclude by outlining the experimental requirements for generating SPCCSs, citing the need for devices that can efficiently produce and measure non-classical properties in specific quantum states. We propose using beam splitter or parametric amplifiers based on nonlinear photonic chips, given their capacity to generate large amounts of non-classical states in multiple output channels. We also examine the statistical analysis of these states, suggesting that machine learning-based methods can be employed to validate the quality of prepared states and measure the accuracy of the generated states. We envision that the development of SPCCSs will contribute to the technological challenges associated with executing interference experiments and coherent communication systems, and provide valuable insights for investigating other complex non-classical states. In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the precise solutions to Einstein's field equations. This review focuses on explaining the fundamental principles and detailed calculations of bivectors within the Newman-Penrose formalism, specifically by converting a complex self-dual electromagnetic field from the standard Minkowski space basis to the complex null tetrad basis. As a result, we derive the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor in the context of Newman-Penrose formalism. A comprehensive overview of the complex coefficients of the conformally unambiguous Weyl tensor in the context of Newman-Penrose formalism is also provided. This involves calculating the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor generated by a complex self-dual electromagnetic field in the context of Newman-Penrose formalism, as well as determining the relationship between this tensor and the Riemann tensor in the complex null tetrad basis. This review is intended for undergraduate students and researchers in the fields of physics and mathematics. Although the use of bivectors involves complex calculations, the underlying principles are straightforward, and the use of Newman-Penrose formalism provides a clear and concise path to the solutions. This review is composed of two parts, the first part is dedicated to introducing the basics of the Newman-Penrose formalism and the complex self-dual electromagnetic field, while the second part delves into the detailed calculations and comprehensive overview mentioned earlier. This review is also applicable to the study of complex spacetimes in the context of General Relativity. This review is the outcome of the author's lecture notes prepared for an undergraduate course titled "General Relativity and Complex Spacetimes" taught at the University of Sri Jayewardenepura, Sri Lanka. This review is unique as it presents the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor in the context of Newman-Penrose formalism, which is an innovative approach that can be further utilized in the analysis of complex spacetimes in the context of General Relativity. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans. These results demonstrate the efficacy of a simplified, CT-only clinical approach for identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus. Our code is available online at this link https://github.com/yousefis/DenseUnet_Esophagus_Segmentation.

Multilingual individuals possess a high level of proficiency in two or more languages, enabling effective written and oral communication across multiple languages. When communicating, they may blend languages, also known as code-switching or code-mixing, by switching between different languages within a single utterance. This research explores current NLP developments, constraints, and potential obstacles in tackling five critical issues affecting multilingual communities: crisis management, healthcare, election campaigns, fake news dissemination, and hate speech. To move forward, we outline potential future datasets, models, and resources to enhance NLP applications for societal betterment, exemplified through an analysis of code-mixing between English and Hindi but with implications for other language combinations. To tackle these challenges, we highlight important considerations and future research opportunities in NLP. To illustrate the potential, we outline a sample dataset annotation framework for code-mixing sentences. To conclude, this paper emphasizes the significance of code-mixing research to preserve multilingual heritage, enabling effective communication and understanding, and facilitating NLP applications that benefit diverse communities, spanning regions with limited resources, culturally complex societies, and multilingual individuals themselves. To move forward, we propose a trajectory for research in code-mixing NLP, focusing on development, evaluation, and real-world implementations, along with a future directory outlining potential research avenues. To thrive, code-mixing NLP must address fundamental challenges in multiple domains, requiring innovative methods to model language, evaluate performance, and validate effectiveness, as well as exploring ways to engage with research communities, incorporating real-world data, and facilitating accessible platforms for resource-constrained regions. To broaden code-mixing research beyond South Asian languages, we stress the importance of describing and standardizing data and models to facilitate reproducibility, enable comparison, and ensure transparency in research methods and results. Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on their similarity to these descriptions. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require more precise guidelines balancing visually impaired users' needs and practical description generation feasibility. High-quality reference data could be ideal for system evaluation, yet we should also consider other alternatives. I discuss practical description evaluation criteria elsewhere in this paper, but other options for evaluating systems using, for example, crowd-sourced ratings or simple metrics like coverage area, are also explored here. Systems' performance can be assessed using these methods before they are applied to real-world applications. I hope this discussion may prompt a shift in focus towards a more flexible, less stringently descriptive system, which could lead to better automatic image description systems. This way, their potential to accurately describe complex images automatically can be unleashed, in turn enabling greater mobility for visually impaired individuals. This paper is organized as follows: I describe the issues with existing human-generated description datasets in Section 2, I discuss suitable evaluation methods for image description systems in Section 3, and I conclude and offer future directions in Section 4. This paper's associated code can be found at https://github.com/alegrosio/evaluating_image_descriptions.

Tantalum oxide compounds, with the formula Ta$_2$O$_5$, are distinguished by unique properties including high dielectric values and minimal reflectivity. Recent studies have also considered Ta$_2$O$_5$ nanoparticles as potential enhancers for hadron therapy treatments of cancer. To understand the material's electronic behavior, researchers have used theoretical simulations from first principles. Yet, Ta$_2$O$_5$ has various forms, complicating attempts to identify their individual features. To resolve this issue, researchers used time-dependent density functional methods to study the energy loss function in Ta$_2$O$_5$, specifically in its optical state, and across different polymorphs. These studies have demonstrated that experimental reflection loss signals can be interpreted assuming that Ta$_2$O$_5$'s $\gamma$-phase represents the primary structure of the material. Notably, researchers have also determined that both the effects of local fields and spin-orbit interactions are vital to correctly determining the energy loss of Ta$_2$O$_5$. Lastly, further validating the $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure, researchers have used a Monte Carlo method to compare calculated reflection loss spectra with the actual results of experiments, achieving a very accurate match. Ultimately, this research has clarified the crystal structure of Ta$_2$O$_5$, and provides a method for predicting its electronic behavior in other situations. Additionally, by extending their analysis to other materials, researchers have also theoretically proven that both Ta$_{2}$O$_{5-x}$N$_x$ and TaN$_{5}$ possess intriguing reflective loss characteristics in the soft X-ray range.

Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. Finally, measures to reduce misinformation dissemination were likely to be less effective in certain state types, such as those composed of independent decision-makers. Our research highlights the significance of The Big Sort in understanding online misinformation dissemination and suggests that reducing geographical segregation may help mitigate the spread of misinformation. Additionally, we provide guidelines for conducting sub-state level analysis, which could be useful for studying the influence of local factors on various social media phenomena beyond The Big Sort. The widespread significance of considering the effect of physical separation in social and online interactions is also discussed. Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not take full advantage of audio feedback from the instructor. To effectively incorporate auditory cues present during demonstrations, understanding their underlying content and purpose is essential. This study examines audio input from humans instructing a robot using Sawyer via spoken language by analyzing three key features: speech duration, tone variation, and speech content. Evaluating these features across four dimensions, it was discovered that instructors frequently use the same vocabulary to describe specific task elements despite varying situations such as task types, audio instructions, and errors encountered during demonstrations. However, differences in speech patterns including duration and inflection are present across these conditions, showing that human speech carries significant, potentially valuable information for enhancing robotic learning through demonstration-based methods. The results of this research can be utilized to design more effective speech-based interfaces for teaching robots in similar contexts. The current study focuses on tasks involving manipulation with the Sawyer robot but its findings are likely applicable to other robotic platforms requiring spoken language instruction. The data collected during the study is available for further analysis by the robotic learning community. The current research paves the way for several potential developments, including designing more efficient speech-based robotic learning interfaces, systems that can correct robotic errors based on audio feedback, and methods for training robots using spoken language in a more adaptive and efficient manner. The study also explores the relationship between human speech and robotic action accuracy, presenting several promising approaches for developing speech-based assessment and evaluation tools for robotic learning. The data presented in this paper can be utilized by researchers to further develop several ongoing projects, including but not limited to Speech-based Robot Evaluation Systems, Adaptive Tutorial Robotic Learning via Spoken Language, and Robotic Error Correction via Auditory Feedback. The current research is an initial step towards a broader project aimed at teaching robots via spoken language, and further development is necessary to tackle its complexities. The findings of this study are validated through a survey administered to human operators in similar contexts. The survey reveals that the instructors' speech patterns are influenced by various factors including their level of expertise and the specific task they are performing, and that the majority of the vocabulary used to describe the tasks is consistent across different conditions. The results of the survey are presented in the supplementary materials available online. The current research was conducted in a controlled environment using a single robot, and further studies are necessary to validate its findings across a broader range of robotic platforms and learning environments. Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing framework for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the key challenges faced in this endeavor. Specifically, we highlight the difficulties in establishing a precise specification for desired system behavior and comparing the meaning of utterances. This paper also introduces a basic prototype of the testing framework, and presents a straightforward approach to comparing utterances. Nevertheless, this approach is acknowledged to have limitations and may lead to false positives in the output. This false positive signal could be mitigated by incorporating additional contextual information, yet this would complicate the process of specifying desired system behavior. This research was conducted as part of the Amazon Alexa Skills Kit Testing Challenge, a competition aimed at identifying an innovative method for evaluating the performance of conversational systems. This challenge initially gained prominence as the Conversational Assistant Testing Challenge at the 2019 International Conference on Automated Testing Embedded Systems. The data sets used in this study are publicly available at Stanford Natural Language Inference, a repository that contains labeled statements about the relationship between utterances. This paper is the expanded version of a previous abstract that was presented at the Conversational Assistant Testing Challenge. This version includes additional details about the testing framework, the challenges faced in developing it, and the approach used to compare the meaning of utterances. This version also clarifies the differences between the two versions of the challenge. This expanded version also includes a section that discusses the related work in the field of conversational system testing. Furthermore, this version outlines the approach that was used to evaluate the performance of a conversational system, and presents empirical evidence that validates the theoretical findings. This version also includes a section that addresses the issues related to the false positive signal and the difficulty of specifying desired system behavior. This version concludes with a section that outlines the future work in the field of conversational system testing. This section includes the development of a more sophisticated approach for comparing the meaning of utterances, the creation of a more comprehensive infrastructure for conversational system testing, and the design of a more challenging protocol for evaluating the performance of conversational systems. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. The proposed approach also gains practical value due to its scalability and potential applicability in various real-world settings. Convex optimization issues often take on a more manageable form when represented with conic formulations that leverage a wide variety of exotic cones. Exotic cones in this context, refer to specialized geometric shapes with properties enabling efficient implementation of computational tools, specifically barrier oracles for their own and dual shapes. This work introduces Hypatia, an interior-point solver designed to handle these complex shapes with ease. Developed using Julia and interfacing with JuMP, Hypatia can utilize a wide assortment of predefined exotic cones. It then generates simplified equivalent formulations for various optimization applications that can provide significant improvements in processing speed and memory consumption. The proposed method demonstrates a marked improvement in problem-solving efficiency when compared to more conventional and complex conic formulations. The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality control pipelines, but effectively generalizing these methods across diverse, previously unseen data remains a significant challenge. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline's performance on multiple large datasets, utilizing ABIDE with 1,102 subjects and CATI-derived data with 9,037 participants for both training and assessment purposes. Our investigation concentrated on MRIQC preprocessing steps and assessed the pipeline's efficacy with and without these preprocessing methods. Further analysis examined site-specific and study-specific classification probabilities for models trained on ABIDE and CATI data without preprocessing. Our primary findings showed that using MRIQC features without preprocessing yielded the best results in models trained and evaluated on diverse, multi-center datasets with varying population characteristics. This led to an improvement in ROC-AUC scores on unseen data of 0.10 when using a subset of the CATI dataset. Nonetheless, models trained on diverse, heterogeneous populations showed questionable generalizability, as evident from site-specific and study-specific probability predictions and derived classification thresholds. This research was conducted in collaboration with the NeuroIMCU project, an initiative aimed at standardizing MRI data analysis and quality control across different studies and institutions. The associated code has been made publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/neuroimcu/mriqc-generalization. To understand how private electric vehicles influence the recovery of power grids following outages, we developed a mathematical framework that incorporates decentralized decision-making in both transportation and energy systems. We utilized multi-agent optimization to model this process and overcame computational challenges through an efficient algorithm based on precise reformation. Numerical analysis was conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, yielding valuable policy insights and paving the way for further study into grid resilience with private EVs within interconnected transportation and energy networks. Ultimately, a robust, user-friendly tool has been created to facilitate management of charging schedules by vehicle owners and grid operators seeking to maximize system stability and efficiency. A case study presented in the appendix highlights the potential for private EVs to influence transportation and energy networks locally, with implications for both transportation and energy policy made clear. With private EV ownership continuing to gain popularity worldwide, understanding the impact of these vehicles on the stability of power grids is increasingly crucial, as noted in studies by the International Energy Agency, the National Renewable Energy Laboratory, and the U.S. Department of Energy. As such, this research provides a foundation for future investigation into various aspects of private EVs and power grid resilience, including but not limited to, battery technology improvements, grid recovery policies, and intersection with public transportation. Furthermore, this work highlights opportunities for energy policymakers, transportation officials, and vehicle manufacturers to collaborate and develop strategies that leverage the benefits of private EVs while minimizing their drawbacks, as shown in the appendix. Lastly, this study offers a framework applicable to various settings, including but not limited to, urban, rural areas, and islands, that can be further adapted to suit local needs. The Motivation Dynamics framework, a concept explored in recent studies that applies bifurcations to model an autonomous agent's decision-making processes, is further developed to accommodate multiple autonomous entities in this paper. We demonstrate how the framework's capabilities can be expanded to capture persistent, cooperative behavior between agents meeting at specific locations, and through in-depth analysis and numerical data, reveal that this extension exhibits a complex pattern indicative of a strange attractor. Ultimately, our research provides a novel explanation for the observed pattern, and highlights the significance of cross-agent interactions in defining both individual and shared trajectories. Moreover, our findings in a realistic simulation setting showcase that agents operating within the Motivation Dynamics framework in a rendezvous scenario with time-based constraints are capable of safely and efficiently cooperating with each other. The development of our model also allows for direct application to cases involving multiple autonomous vehicles in a rendezvous scenario, as demonstrated in a real-world air traffic control context. Utilizing the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we've developed a method to calculate weak lensing convergence by combining data on the positions and photometry of foreground galaxies. A correlation between this approach and the residual Hubble diagram values of Type Ia supernovae holds a $3.6\sigma$ significance and is consistent with dark matter effects due to galactic halos. Furthermore, we constrained galactic halo properties, including the mass-to-light ratio $\Gamma$ and the radial distribution of matter density within haloes $\rho(r)$. Based on this analysis, we formulated an equation to calculate the lens-induced additional random scattering in SN Ia magnitudes: $\sigma_{\rm lens} = (0.06 \pm 0.017) \cdot (d_{\rm C}(z)/ d_{\rm C}(1))^{3/2}$. As a result, the lens-induced apparent magnitude dispersion will approach the same magnitude as intrinsic SN Ia scatter at $z \approx 1.2$. Building upon this research, we propose an adjusted estimator for SN Ia distance moduli that incorporates the effects of lensing and is calculable using existing observational data, thereby potentially enhancing the precision of cosmological parameter inference from high-redshift SN Ia data. Greater precision can be achieved with higher spatial resolution galaxy surveys and better photometric data, such as those provided by the James Webb Space Telescope, its successors, and similar missions. Ultimately, this research highlights a previously underutilized source of information that can be extracted from Pantheon SN Ia data and similar datasets, offering a promising approach to investigating the distribution of matter within galactic haloes and improving the accuracy of cosmological parameter inference from SN Ia data.

The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process. We also investigated the effects of charge control methods on the reduction of spectral diffusion-induced losses and explored the potential of T centers for quantum optical elements, including the integration of multiple T centers within a single photonic device. Overall, our findings indicate that SOI materials offer significant advantages over bulk silicon, providing a more reliable and efficient means of creating high T center densities that are crucial for solid-state and integrated quantum technology applications. A key obstacle in kidney transplants arises from the incompatibility between donors and patients, which has been exacerbated by the growing scarcity of kidney donors. Desensitization techniques were developed to overcome the immunological difficulties. Patients receiving incompatible transplants face a higher risk of transplant rejection, infections, and cancer, and are more likely to lose their transplants. We aim to find the optimal acceptance criteria for end-stage kidney patients by potentially receiving incompatible kidneys. A Markov Decision Process model is introduced, which accounts for the level of incompatibility as a key factor, making it a more complex problem to solve, but with suitable conditions, it is possible to establish control limit policies that can be easily applied. Our study uses numerical examples to demonstrate how the optimal policy behaves under different levels of incompatibility, and highlights the significance of taking incompatibility into consideration in decision-making, especially when desensitization treatments are available. We also explore various levels of incompatibility to demonstrate how it affects the value function and the optimal acceptance policy, which can be seen as a key contribution to this research. The results show that the usual "control limit" policy is not generally effective when incompatibility is significant, which may lead to suboptimal outcomes, with the premium for accepting an incompatible kidney increasing exponentially as the level of incompatibility also becomes more significant. The marginal benefit of accepting an incompatible kidney reduces as the level of incompatibility increases, which is a crucial finding that has implications for patient management, and highlights the importance of considering transplanted kidneys of any level of incompatibility, especially those that are moderately incompatible, as long as sufficient follow-up care is provided. The study also highlights the opportunity to recover some of the premium for treating highly incompatible patients, which has implications for healthcare management. The paper concludes by highlighting the opportunity for further research into more complex models that can be used to guide patient management and treatment decisions in kidney transplants. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. Our work also explores different model variants, places our findings within the broader context of thematic analysis, and examines the relationship between company names and the words that describe them. Our study concludes by outlining potential future directions for improving these models, including the difficult task of uncovering the non-linear, time-varying relationships between the distribution of terms and the hidden semantic structures. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghassab/word-embeddings-explained. Our data is available at https://data.mendeley.com/datasets/9wvzkgkw68/datasets. Our results are also illustrated in the accompanying paper titled: The Dynamic Co-Loading Problem. Or in short: How we learned to stop fearing word2vec and love Markov's eyes rolled back in surprise! This article presents the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based IDET systems as alternatives to our previously proposed optimal wideband waveforming strategy in [1].
Fair-throughput and sum-throughput optimisation problems are defined and formulated.
By leveraging an algorithm that utilizes fixed points, we derive the optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput values for SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems. 
A hybrid fast time-diviation multiple access (FTD-MTA) scheme is proposed to implement the optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput values in practice.
In the FTD-MTA scheme, the rate of time division must match the rate of channel variation, thereby creating an opportunity for power and subcarrier optimization, which in turn leads to an increase in energy and data transfer rates.
Simulation results confirm the effectiveness of the SISO-OFDM, MISO-OFDM, and the FTD-MTA schemes in enhancing the energy and data transfer rates beyond multiple antennas and multiple carriers. 
The proposed SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems can be applied to integrated base stations in cellular networks, wind-solar energy systems, and radio frequency (RF) energy harvesting systems. 
The MATLAB code for the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems is available online at [2].

This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, we've developed a numerical strategy utilizing Cartesian grids to efficiently handle complex boundary transformations and high-resolution interface representation. This method enables a second-order conservative numerical scheme and has been effectively applied to solve various problems, including Stefan problems, dendrite growth, and Rayleigh--B\'enard instabilities, even in the presence of melting boundaries. Furthermore, we've compared our results to existing literature, demonstrating close agreement and improving the resolution of certain phenomena. To accommodate moving boundaries, we've introduced a novel treatment of the phase change condition that eliminates the need for artificial thin layers, even in the presence of strong temperature gradients. This approach has been implemented in a code dubbed `admelt`, and we've analyzed the computational efficiency and accuracy of this code through a range of numerical experiments. This has implications for the study of melting problems, offering a more practical and numerically rigorous approach, and we believe this method has value for contributing to a broader community interested in level-set and phase field techniques. In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior that steers clear of dominated actions is another key goal. However, existing algorithms in the general multiplayer games scenario require an exponentially large number of samples relative to the number of players to determine rationalizable equilibria when working under bandit feedback. This research develops an initial suite of efficient algorithms to learn both Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) that achieve polynomial sample complexities in line with problem parameters including the number of players. It also includes an enhanced approach for identifying a rationalizable action profile with a significantly improved sample requirement, exceeding the current benchmark established in 2021. Our innovative solutions involve the integration of multiple cutting-edge techniques that concurrently ensure the rationalizability and absence of (swap-)regret through correlated exploration and dynamic learning rate adjustments, offering potential value as standalone contributions. Moreover, our results are complemented by a sample complexity lower bound, underscoring the precision of the devised guarantees. This study is further distinguished by the incorporation of a rationalization-focused counterpart within the framework of online learning, resulting in a novel formulation with a previously established guarantee. Lastly, our results for the offline setting are extendable to offline learning settings with a associated generalization barrier introduced in 2021. This research is accompanied by an accompanying online learning variant, an analytical characterizations of the underlying structure, and a specific game scenario, all yielding actionable policy recommendations. The underlying problems and techniques are also visualized through multiple figures. This work is relevant to a broader context discussed in Section 1.3. This paper is organized as follows: the problem is formalized in Section 2, an initial algorithm is presented in Section 3, a more efficient version is developed in Section 4, an adaptive approach is introduced in Section 5, an online variant is discussed in Section 6, and an analysis of the specified structure and an offline setting with generalization are explored in Section 7. All together, this research develops a pioneering approach for discovering rationalizable action profiles in multiagent learning settings, an achievement that is complemented by an underlying structure and extension to offline learning with generalization, both accounted for in Section 7. This work is concluded by Section 8. All algorithms and results mentioned in this paper are validated through multiple simulated scenarios. An analysis of a stochastic Susceptible to Infective to Recovered model is conducted, where the model is based on an Erdős-Rényi random graph that changes dynamically as susceptible individuals connected to infected neighbours form new connections or sever existing ones. As the model is scaled to accommodate large populations, researchers obtained mathematical proofs of key properties of the model, particularly its early stages and the phase where the epidemic spreads rapidly. They also found that under certain conditions, there are sharp thresholds where the model suddenly switches between two completely different behaviours. It has been proven that these transitions are more dramatic if the model is changed to only form new connections to uninfected individuals, where the model suddenly switches from no infections to complete spread. This model is equivalent to a specific version of the classic birth-death process, where it results in a discrete process that is approximated by a continuous process with a sharp threshold where the process suddenly switches from no infections to complete spread. This was previously conjectured by Dunlap and Allen, who also proposed a related question about the model that forms new connections randomly, without considering the infection status of the other end of the connection. This question is answered by providing an estimate of the time it takes to reach a fully infected state, as well as the shape of the curve that describes this time against a key parameter of the model. This was previously unknown and was conjectured by one of the authors in 2017. Although developed with primary focus on PDF fitting, this pipeline can be utilized by any research group working on phenomenological studies. We introduce MG-GLAM, a computational tool developed to rapidly create comprehensive N-body simulations for various cosmological theories, specifically modified gravity models. This program builds upon the existing GLAM code and incorporates an advanced multigrid method to solve the non-linear equations characteristic of modified gravity theories, resulting in highly efficient simulations. For $f(R)$ gravity, MG-GLAM includes multiple variations that mimic distinct behaviors of these models and offers tailored algorithms to maintain speed and precision. The code excels at producing a broad spectrum of modified gravity simulations and offers significant computational benefits, outperforming existing N-body simulations by a factor of over a hundred while yielding accurate results for key cosmological metrics. MG-GLAM is suited for creating large sets of modified gravity simulations that can be utilized in mock galaxy catalogues and emulators for ongoing and future galaxy surveys. The code is available for download at [www.mgglam.com]. Published in 2018.

Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals, respectively. Ultimately, these pairings yield domains that evolve in time and associated Gaussian free fields. We observe these domains to be composed of multiple growing branches that stem from the origin. This development generalizes the original result of Miller and Sheffield to multiple SLE, and it provides a constructive approach to defining imaginary surfaces evolving in time. Furthermore, this work provides a probabilistic interpretation of multiple SLE as an imaginary surface evolving in time, with the associated Gaussian free field given by harmonic measure. This finding is particularly evident in the case of SLE$_\kappa$ for $\kappa\geq 4$ when the process is driven by the Beta$(4-\kappa,2)$ process. This information is unavailable through classical approaches using Loewner equations. Specifically, this provides us with information about the statistics of SLE branches, which is directly related to the statistics of the associated Gaussian free field. This change in behavior is induced by a change in the statistics of the underlying random process, which itself resides in the domain whose behavior it is attempting to model. Furthermore, the results from the model matched the outcomes from the LES simulations, confirming its effectiveness. Improving neural conversational agents' ability to produce diverse, engaging responses in casual conversations is a challenge. To tackle this issue, this paper introduces two significant innovations. Firstly, it proposes a new assessment metric that employs Natural Language Inference to gauge the semantic variety of responses generated by the model in a conversation. Using a previously established framework, this metric was tested and showed a clear connection between Natural Language Inference Diversity and semantic variety. It was discovered that the contradiction relation yields more precise results than the neutral relation in measuring diversity and integrating the NLI model's confidence achieves the highest performance to date. Secondly, this paper demonstrates a way to enhance the semantic variety of responses generated by the model through an iterative procedure called Diversity Threshold Generation, which, in comparison to standard generation methods, results in an average 137% improvement in NLI Diversity. Moreover, this approach was integrated into a renowned conversational agent evaluation metric and yielded a 25% increase in Semantic Variety. The code for this research has been made publically available at the following link: https://github.com/ParthGhosh/NLI_Diversity.

The occurrence of sustainable hydrogen burning in very low-mass stars might be impacted by rotation due to the addition of centrifugal force and potential break-up caused by rapid spinning. Computer simulations model rotating low-mass stars with the capability for sustained nuclear reactions, considering a range of rotation rates, rather than slow rotation alone. Using these simulations, we determined the boundaries within which stars could maintain nuclear energy through hydrogen burning. These boundaries varied based on angular momentum. However, above a certain threshold (approximately 8.85 x 10^48 erg s) the boundaries broke into two distinct branches, resulting from objects losing mass and experiencing extreme spin. This research was applied to model the development of sub-stellar objects. Two possible scenarios were modeled: one with external forces gradually slowing the star, mainly controlled by spin-down time, and another where the star spins out of control, ultimately shedding mass and shrinking. In the second scenario, the simulation stopped at the point mass shedding began, as it required the inclusion of hydrodynamic interactions with surface convolutions. Despite this limitation, notable outcomes were observed for both cases. In the controlled spin-down scenario, the relationship between angular velocity and angular momentum followed the predicted pattern. In the uncontrolled scenario, the simulation showed two possible points where mass shedding could occur, representing a hysteresis loop. This loop suggests that the stable range for these objects behaves similarly to a dip in the Roche lobe, although this assumption requires confirmation through the inclusion of surface convolutions and hydrodynamics. This behavior has significant implications for theories related to low-mass star formation, as it suggests that objects within this range could be unstable by nature, and therefore any formed within this stable range may survive for a significant amount of time. This potential stability is further supported by its similarity to the known hysteresis loops that low-mass stars experience during radial pulsations, as seen in the way their stable ranges behave. This could also be relevant to exoplanet research, as it provides a possible explanation for the occurrence of pulsations in some exoplanets. This theory is particularly significant because it could influence our understanding of objects with masses between those of planets and stars, as it suggests that objects with this mass behavior are actually very low-mass stars rather than exoplanets. A new model based on a comprehensive expression for radiation energy has been proposed, and it effectively elucidates the dynamics of afterglows in multiple contexts, including relativistic, non-relativistic phases and fireball radiations with radiative and adiabatic components. By utilizing this novel model, comprehensive and detailed analyses have been conducted on various afterglow phenomena, including the modification of shockwave dynamics, particle acceleration, and the interplay between radiative and adiabatic energies within jets. These investigations have been extended to examine afterglow dynamics in multiple scenarios, including: (1) an expanding shockwave in a stellar wind, (2) a decelerating shockwave within a dense medium, (3) circular shocks within a topologically flat space-time, and (4) an accelerating GRB jet within a radiative and adiabatic context. Furthermore, this model has been applied to predict observable afterglow signals, including the modification of the characteristic radiated energies, luminosities, and spectral distributions across various frequencies. These predictions have been compared to extensive numerical simulations, and they exhibit a satisfactory match, thereby providing a straightforward analytical understanding of afterglow dynamics. Ultimately, this research has implications for interpreting afterglow observations, both currently available and forthcoming, and it has significant potential to aid in a deeper understanding of high-energy astrophysical phenomena, including GRBs, mergers, and supernovae. This work has been further extended to examine the effects of both matter and energy injections into afterglows, and it has been found that such injections can manifest as multiple episodes of afterglow activity, thereby providing a possible explanation for recurring fast X-ray transient phenomena, and it has been predicted that such afterglow scenarios could give rise to a population of previously undiscovered, faint GRBs. This research has been supplemented by an exhaustive bibliography, and it has been organized into six individual chapters, each of which is self-contained. This document is intended for researchers, scientists, and students interested in high-energy astrophysics, particularly in the dynamics of GRB-afterglows, and it has been published in the American Institute of Physics.

To achieve this, we will create a mediator filter utilizing reference governors to ensure that performance constraints are met. Due to the impacts and adjustments made during the gait cycle causing deviations from desired periodic orbits, we will ensure robust hybrid invariance through the application of predictive methods within a short timeframe. This discovery motivated further research into the properties of a specific mathematical theory related to valued fields. In the course of these investigations, the authors proved that this theory does not have a certain desirable feature and demonstrated that, for infinite fields $k$, the associated power series fields cannot be computationally decided. This, in turn, led to an analogous undecidability conclusion for a specific complex-valued field of power series. The article at hand provides an introductory overview of this research and the associated mathematical concepts, covering topics from algebra, analysis, and mathematical logic. The main results of Becker, Denef, and Lipschitz, as well as additional relevant information, are also included. The paper was originally published in 1989 as part of the Proceedings of the International Congress of Mathematicians in Kyoto. The associated journal article also considered a related algebraic field and found that its properties could be characterized by a specific polynomial equation, thereby extending the results of the original 1979 findings. The article in its current form has been updated to include a 1994 appendix addressing the issue of quantifier elimination for a specific type of field. The original publication can be found in the journal Advances in Mathematics, with volume and page numbers [28, 133-153] and [28, 155-160]. The copyright for the paper is held by Elsevier. The first, titled "Note 1", discusses an approach to proving the undecidability of a specific field using a recursive set and a theorem from R. L. Baker. The second, titled "Note 2", explores the connection between the theoretical results and the actual computational processes, and the challenges of implementing the total residue map due to its complex nature. M. de Jeu, along with the contributions of S. J. Melvin and the unknown contributor of the note titled "Valued fields with a total residue map: Note 2".

In order to enhance side-channel attacks, this research introduces a new technique, HyperDegrade, which incorporates previous methods and employs simultaneous multithreading architectures.  A novel analysis into the causes of performance degradation through cache eviction was also performed, leading to the discovery of an unknown source of slowdowns.  Compared to existing techniques, HyperDegrade resulted in more significant slowdowns and improvements, which in certain cases achieved an enhanced time granularity of three orders of magnitude for Flush+Reload attacks.  To further evaluate the technique, metrics for side-channel leakage were proposed, which demonstrated that HyperDegrade could be effective in side-channel amplification without compromising data integrity.  A fair comparison between three different performance degradation strategies in combination with Flush+Reload attacks revealed HyperDegrade's efficacy, which enabled the development of an attack on an OpenSSL vulnerability three times more efficient than other methods.  In addition, HyperDegrade's applicability to Raccoon-like attacks was also demonstrated, which can succeed with real-world data and extend the scope of existing attacks to various protocols, filling in the gap left by previous research.  All of the research's source code has been made available publicly.

In cooperative systems with multiple agents, coordination enables tasks to be performed that would be beyond the capabilities of any single agent. We investigate the concept of coordination through strategic decision-making, focusing on a scenario where agents select between two tasks of varying difficulty that are randomly distributed and partially known. It has been found that a stable state of cooperation, characterized by a straightforward linear pattern, can be achieved when there is a wide range of possible task difficulties. Furthermore, it was discovered that the most advantageous action for each agent in response to an approachable strategy profile can be complex and nonlinear when the distribution of task difficulties is not uniform. A computational method has been established to calculate a cooperative equilibrium through learning within the set of linear policy options. Lastly, both theoretical and simulation-based evidence demonstrate that, when tasks are uniformly distributed, the most advantageous action for each agent in response to an approachable strategy profile can be a simple nonlinear pattern. This research was presented at the IEEE Conference on Decision and Control and the IEEE/RSJ-GI International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems in 2018 and 2019 respectively.

Based on how entities cooperate, FL can be categorized into two primary forms - horizontal and vertical FL. The former involves participants who collaborate using identical data attributes, while in the latter, entities with overlapping sample IDs collaborate using different features. Network vulnerability assessment is crucial for creating strategies to prevent the spread of malicious information and diseases in networks. Researchers often study network immunization, but traditional approaches typically focus on broad measures, such as network criticality and component size. In contrast, this paper delves into a micro-level analysis, where the removal of individual nodes during an attack is examined in detail. Based on percolation theory, the authors analyze the effects of removing a single node that causes other nodes to disconnect from the main component. Specifically, this paper investigates the number of nodes that become disconnected from the main component as a result of removing one node. By applying this micro-level approach to a random attack on a Cayley tree network, the distribution of the resulting node removal sizes is derived. Furthermore, a critical threshold exists below which a single node's removal results in the disappearance of the large component, and an analytical expression for this threshold is provided. Additionally, a probabilistic criterion is established to determine the nodes most likely to cause the loss of the large component. Theoretical findings are validated through numerical simulations of random attacks on Cayley tree networks. The implications of these results for network security and epidemiology applications are also discussed. The approach and findings presented in this paper can be extended to other network types. The detection capabilities of advanced gravitational wave detectors are hindered in the high-frequency range by the quantum limitations of measurement and signal loss in optical recycling systems. Overcoming this constraint is critical for identifying gravitational waves generated by binary neutron star mergers. We present the concept of the sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, an innovative variation of the Michelson design where the end mirrors are optically linked to form an additional resonating cavity. By transforming the detector into a system with multiple coupled cavities, this design outperforms the conventional signal-recycled Michelson setup by overcoming optical loss-induced limitations. Using advanced parameters similar to LIGO+, this new design offers improved sensitivity at high frequencies or better signal-to-noise ratios for specific binary neutron star merger waveforms, offering promising possibilities for future gravitational wave detectors. Although this topology has been technically feasible since 2007, it was previously overlooked in the search for innovative designs. This new design also incorporates a variant known as the annular Sagnac interferometer, which provides a more straightforward approach to overcoming loss-induced limitations, offering comparable advantages with simpler parameters. Both variants have been analyzed using numerical simulations, along with a discussion of the proposed implementation and the challenges it faces.

Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to better performance, but our findings suggest that $n$-gram models still excel in many situations with low computational costs, demonstrating a strong foundation of language understanding. Building upon this discovery, we developed a neural model that learns from the remaining knowledge between $n$-gram models and the true language distribution, allowing for both a deeper grasp of language and the flexibility to adjust models through the $n$-gram base without altering the neural model. Through extensive experiments on tasks including language modeling, machine translation, and summarization, our hybrid approach consistently delivers enhanced performance over standard neural models and facilitates seamless domain adaptation by simply swapping the $n$-gram base, eliminating the need for additional training. Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a face that varies based on the orientation and another face that remains invariant, then fuses these faces via a self-alignment mechanism informed by occlusion. Exhaustive testing of our proposed technique on the widely used AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets shows substantial performance enhancements over existing top-ranking methods. Moreover, our proposed approach demonstrates robustness in face reconstruction and dense alignment on the COFP dataset tailored for head poses and in scenarios with partial face occlusions. Our code has been made publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyangDeng/SADRNet.

Researchers examined marked ordered trees with the ability to designate some right edges as "optional", given they don't lead to leaf nodes. They employed this model to analyze skew Dyck paths. A key aspect studied was the number of deepest nodes in these marked trees. Through explicit generating functions, they obtained insights, revealing the average number of deepest nodes converges to $\frac53$ as the number of nodes increases, which can be contrasted to standard ordered trees with a convergent average of $2$ deepest nodes. This result is interesting as it provides a precise characterisation of the integer sequence associated with the number of deepest nodes in marked ordered trees, offering a mathematical context that may be relevant to certain statistical or combinatorial applications. The associated integer sequence, denoted as $c_n$, is linked to the number of skew Dyck paths ending at level $n$ without an immediate descent to level $n+1$, and can be distinguished from other related sequences such as the Bessel numbers or the Gruenberg-Hall numbers. Furthermore, the integral representation of $c_n$ enables the derivation of explicit formulas for the number of deepest nodes in marked trees with a specified height or number of leaves. The studied sequence also extends to marked ordered trees with designated leaf nodes, providing a general framework that can be applied to other combinatorial objects, and the introduced approach can be used to enumerate the number of deepest nodes in various models, offering a powerful tool for its own sake. A key factor for maintaining stability in future low-carbon power grids is expected to be energy storage systems. Studies examining past experiences reveal a common issue with storage units - they frequently fail to take advantage of high-price signals during periods of low energy supply. This behavior has been often attributed to inaccurate forecasting or operational issues. However, our research suggests a more plausible explanation is rooted in risk-averse decision-making practices. Utilizing a stochastic self-scheduling approach and real data from the Australian electricity market, our findings show that risk-conscious storage units prioritize short-term cost savings by engaging in local price speculation, and tend to ignore opportunities in periods with unusual price fluctuations. This has significant policy implications, given the difficulty of detecting and managing storage units' risk aversion. Moreover, it highlights the risk of storage units contributing to market instability and unusual price patterns. This study also highlights the challenge of predicting storage units' behavior and the need for new regulatory frameworks that account for their risk-averse characteristics. Our investigation focused on the transport properties of HgTe quantum wells near their critical thickness, where the energy gap is minimal, and the energy spectrum is described by a singular Dirac cone structure. Both large and small-sized (mesoscopic) samples were examined as part of this study. When looking at small-sized samples, a well-defined, quantized resistance emerged at low magnetic field strength due to Landau filling, and was closely related to helical edge states that form around the neutral point of the samples. Conversely, larger samples showed significant resistance oscillations in low-magnetic-field conditions. This behavior is attributed to interaction between the neutral state at the edge and a non-neutral hole Landau level within the bulk material. A hypothetical model incorporating a reservoir formed by heavy holes has been developed as an explanatory framework. This model highlights the importance of magnetic field-induced coupling between this reservoir and the free electrons within the bulk material. As a result, a more comprehensive understanding of transport properties in these gapless quantum wells is gained, and examination of their edges and body remains a promising area of investigation. Furthermore, the examination of transport properties in these samples offers a unique perspective on their low-dimensional physics. This study was conducted using experimental transport data obtained in HgTe quantum wells of varying thickness, and incorporates theoretical calculations of quantum transport, edge states, and the energy gap vs. thickness. The examination of these calculations provides insight into the underlying physics of these materials, and examines the effects of screening on the neutral state and resulting edge states. The examination of heavy hole Landau levels within the bulk material is also discussed.
