In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), individual cells can schedule uplink and downlink modes independently, depending on local traffic conditions, but this causes interference between neighboring cells, turning a critical problem into an NP-hard mixed-integer non-convex challenge. We've developed an efficient and localized solution, separating power allocation and scheduling processes, first assigning power independently to cells, followed by a non-cooperative game determining scheduling modes, with payoffs calculated according to the level of interference and required cell communication. Simulations, set in an outdoor scenario with multiple small cells, reveal our method outperforms static TDD solutions. Additionally, we find that in areas with low mobility, better communication in scheduling modes can come at the expense of communication speed, requiring careful balance in such situations. Moreover, our solution can be implemented using existing Base Station technology, with minimal computational requirements. We also present a key cell case study, facilitating understanding of our general findings. Overall, our work provides a practical and efficient TDD solution, capable of adapting to dynamic cellular environments.

In this work, we introduce a novel meta-learning framework centered on ODE neural networks, which acquires an understanding of gradients. This framework grants optimizers enhanced flexibility and infuses an automatic inductive bias into tasks, as we have found. Through the simplest Hamiltonian Neural Network implementation, our method proves more effective than a comparable LSTM-based meta-learner for a simulated task and MNIST with ReLU activations in the model being optimized, as well as consistently outperforming traditional optimization techniques for the artificial task and delivering results on par with standard optimization for MNIST. Nonetheless, more complex Hamiltonian Neural Networks fail to match the performance of traditional optimization for MNIST. This research also highlights issues with existing works applying gradient-based meta-learning within the context of Hamiltonian Neural Networks. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghaleee/gradient-learning-by-hamm.

Simply enhancing a machine learning model's accuracy is not sufficient, as we must also focus on increasing its reliability. This consideration is crucial for creating robust AI systems that are capable of withstanding critical situations in areas like transportation, finance, and medical fields. We recommend developing a collaborative multi-agent framework that combines artificial intelligence with human input. This proposed system involves two key components: a scoring agent that calculates a reliability metric for each prediction, penalizing both overoptimistic and overly cautious results; and a refinement agent that utilizes a set of human-defined safety guidelines to identify and rectify unusual instances. It then uses these corrected examples to update its model through transfer learning. We put the proposed system through testing on datasets modified to contain artificial errors and found that it effectively improves both the accuracy and reliability of the model with only a limited increase in training data. Furthermore, the proposed system demonstrates significant advantages over conventional approaches to model reliability, demonstrating its potential to be a versatile and adaptable solution. The code for this project is available at https://github.com/HappySong-VSU/HITL-AI-model-trustworthiness.

A newly defined polynomial, referred to as the nth toroidal colored Jones polynomial, is established for links in a thickened torus. Dubbed $J_n^T$, this polynomial demonstrates numerous properties similar to the original colored Jones polynomial, and notably displays volume conjecture behavior. By applying $J_n^T$, we prove the volume conjecture holds true for a specific link, and provide computational data suggesting it holds for additional links. Moreover, $J_n^T$ can be represented through two distinct constructions, a pseudo-operator invariant, and a construction rooted in the Kauffman bracket skein module of the torus. Notably, $J_n^T$ yields invariants for virtual and biperiodic links, providing an instance of volume conjecture behavior in a virtual link. Lastly, $J_n^T$ can be interpreted as a comprehensive version of the trivalent volume conjecture, providing a precise formula for the coefficients of some roots of its associated polynomial. This is achieved through the application of combinatorial enumeration principles, specifically the Fibonacci numbers and Eulerian numbers, and confirms the volume conjecture holds true for specific links, including the trefoil and the figure-eight. This is also shown to be equivalent to a specific colored hyperboloid, and through a change of variables, yields a polynomial of a form previously unknown in the context of the volume conjecture. The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in this area, with several strategies being developed to combine structured knowledge for enhanced performance.  Additionally, multiple data augmentation techniques have been discovered to be valuable tools in natural language processing tasks.  Building on prior work incorporating BERT and WordNet knowledge, this study explores various data augmentation techniques in context-gloss pairs to enhance the efficacy of WSD.  Experimental results indicate that both sentence and word-level augmentation strategies are effective in addressing WSD, while the incorporation of hypernyms' definitions from a lexical knowledge base can further improve performance.  A comparative analysis of different context-gloss augmentation techniques is conducted, revealing that the application of back translation to definitions produces the most satisfactory outcomes.  A modulated model incorporating the most successful techniques achieves the best results, with a score of 80.3% on the SENSEVAL.  A tool has been made available online for generating context-gloss pairs via word-level augmentation.  This study also presents a roadmap for incorporating additional knowledge into context-gloss pairs to enhance the efficacy of WSD.  A comparative study with leading WSD models is conducted, showing that the modulated model's performance is on par with state-of-the-art models when considering the computational expenses involved.  A further examination is carried out to determine whether BERT's capacity to differentiate word senses is reliant on the availability of context-gloss pairs, leading to the discovery that BERT is capable of distinguishing senses even in the absence of such pairs, even when the gap between senses is linguistically incidental.  A related issue, namely the difficulty of accessing definitions for words with multiple senses, is addressed in order to further examine this challenge.  A novel methodology is presented for generating definitions for words with multiple senses, along with empirical results confirming the uniqueness of the definitions generated and the relationship between the definitions and existing lexical knowledge bases.  A further analysis is conducted to determine the relationship between the difficulty of defining words and the difficulty of disambiguating them, leading to the discovery that there is no correlation between these two difficulties.  A theoretical discussion is also presented on the difficulty of defining words, along with a taxonomy of difficult definitions.  A challenge remains in developing a uniform and universally applicable methodology for defining words, although the diversity of definitions is considered a beneficial aspect of words. This study focuses on key elements in cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing, specifically schema linking and value filling. To enhance encoding abilities, a column selection auxiliary task is proposed, leveraging explicit targets for relevance matching. Additionally, two value filling approaches are presented to bridge the gap between current zero-shot parsers and practical applications, considering that many existing parsers overlook value filling in synthesized SQL. Experiments on the Spider dataset demonstrate the superiority of our proposed framework over baseline models in terms of execution and exact set match accuracy when database contents are inaccessible, with further analysis pointing to areas for future improvement. Moreover, our proposed framework showcases versatility in real-world settings, outperforming state-of-the-art zero-shot parsers while requiring minimal additional training data for domain adaptation. The code is available at https://github.com/ChenXudong123/End-to-End-Text-to-SQL.

This paper delves into the utilization of differential privacy within the framework of graph-based data. It outlines the DP formulations relevant to publishing graphs, statistical analysis associated with graphs, and machine learning on graph-based data, including graph neural networks. However, applying DP to graph data poses significant challenges due to interconnected data points that can form complex relationships. This issue is compounded by a lack of universally accepted DP formulation in graph-based contexts. This problem further exacerbates the difficulty in conducting private machine learning on graph data. A notable absence of systematised research on graph-based learning in relation to privacy was a key driver of our work, leading us to explore various formulations of DP on graphs, discuss associated challenges and promising applications including GNNs. This work also compares and distinguishes different graph-based learning tasks from those that incorporate graph neural networks. Ultimately, our work is concluded by examining open research questions and exploring possible avenues for further investigation in this domain. This paper is the outcome of a research project aimed at understanding the utilisation of private graph-based learning within the realm of social network data. Researchers have successfully used hydrodynamic theories to simulate complex dynamics of quantum many-body systems, and in this work, we've developed a novel stochastic hydrodynamic approach for describing interacting Bose gases within a specific phase-space framework. This method extends previous hydrodynamic methods, enabling the simulation of a system's full quantum dynamics and allowing for the calculation of non-equilibrium correlations, even for short-wavelength phenomena. Building upon this description, we derived a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic model that simulates long-lasting non-equilibrium situations while sacrificing a more precise quantum fluctuation treatment, and found it to be directly connected with the established Bogoliubov approach. Furthermore, we applied and validated our method by investigating a quantum shock wave scenario and comparing its outcomes to existing quantum many-body theories. The developed phase-space stochastic hydrodynamic model proves beneficial for studying open quantum systems involving interacting Bose gases, and serves as a valuable bridge between hydrodynamic theories and quantum many-body phenomena. The developed model has a 'hydrodynamical' regime, and we demonstrated that it extends the existing Bogoliubov approach, enabling a deeper analysis of correlations in interacting systems. The model's capabilities in simulating systems' full quantum dynamics also make it suited for investigating specific situations, such as sound wave propagation in a Bose-Einstein condensate driven by a laser. The model can be applied to realistic situations by solving the stochastic hydrodynamic equations numerically, and we showed this in our shock wave scenario investigation. The developed model offers a practical solution for simulating systems on a computer, and our code is available publicly. The model's extension of the Bogoliubov approach and its predictive power for open quantum systems, combined with its practical implementation, provides a valuable research tool for theoretical physicists. The developed model can simulate situations that the Bogoliubov approach cannot, and our calculations on model parameters showed how its predictions change compared to the Bogoliubov approach. We define a new concept of relative 1-homotopy type for mappings between a surface and a metric space that contains a specified set of Jordan curves, and investigate its properties. This enables us to prove the existence and local smoothness of the surfaces with minimal area within a particular relative 1-homotopy class in certain types of metric spaces. Furthermore, we establish that when the ambient space has a certain topological characteristic, maps that are relatively 1-homotopic are also relatively homotopic. These findings also hold for closed surfaces and improve previous results of several mathematicians. Additionally, we provide a specific instance of a scenario where relative 1-homotopy does not imply homotopy, and offer an alternative proof of a result previously obtained by Korelka. A special case of our results concerning surfaces in a Euclidean space is also presented. Lastly, we discuss the relationship between relative 1-homotopy type and a different topological concept, and offer an additional theorem that can be found in the work of Mirzaei.

Recent studies on the 64Ni nucleus with a low-spin structure have provided significant insights: combining data from four experiments allowed researchers to identify several 0+ and 2+ excited states below 4.5 MeV, and characterize their properties. Using a Monte Carlo shell model, scientists were able to explain the findings and uncover a surprisingly intricate pattern of shapes existing together, where a high-energy prolate 0+ state at 3463 keV, and a collective 2+ state just above it, 286 keV, marked a first in Ni isotopes. This discovery in Ni isotopes, combined with previous findings in 48Ca and 70Zn, supports the predictive power of three-major shell-model interactions, and highlight the importance of the monopole tensor interaction in driving shape coexistence. The unique pattern of levels in 64Ni also differs from that in 72Ni, demonstrating that the same combination of interactions that lead to coexistence in lighter isotopes, can result in distinct phenomena in heavier ones, where other factors like pairing and single-particle energies play a significant role. The exclusive use of monopole components in the tensor interaction, combined with its substantial strength, also stands out in this study, and could have implications for similar phenomena in other nuclei. The detailed data and theoretical analysis provided an unusually clear picture of 64Ni's structure, offering potential insights for theories of effective interactions, and others that rely on 64Ni's properties, such as the neutrinoless koherent electron scattering experiment. The distinctive pattern of levels in 64Ni also offers a unique opportunity to understand the role of the monopole tensor interaction in driving low-spin shape coexistence, and to anticipate this phenomenon in other Ni and closed-shell nuclei, where the motion of neutrons and protons in the fpg shell can result in 0+ and 2+ collective states at low energies. Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are excessively sensitive to the manner in which the data is divided, often resulting in suboptimal solutions and significant difficulties in achieving reproducibility. In contrast, our research suggests employing the reduced variance j-k fold CV method, which involves conducting multiple independent assessments across K subgroups within the training set J times. The aim is to mitigate performance estimation's intrinsic instability and facilitate effective parameter tuning by prioritizing variance minimization over bias. In line with this principle, our study advocates for a smaller K than typically adopted and instead invests computational resources in increasing the value of J, as demonstrated across diverse NLP tasks including sentiment analysis, part-of-speech tagging and text classification. In one representative example, reducing K from 10 to 5 led alone for a specific model and task, without changing J, resulted in a 20 times decrease in the time consumed. Furthermore, our findings show that the recently introduced Hyperband method often yields optimal results when combined with the minimalist j-k = 5 x 5 CV setting. In summary, our research highlights the importance of balancing both variance and bias when employing CV for tuning deep NLP models, as well as the widespread adaptability of the reduced variance j-k fold CV method across diverse applications. Deep Neural Networks with vast parameters have faced challenges in real-time deployment, prompting the utilization of Teacher-Student architectures in knowledge distillation. Initially used to achieve comparable performance with smaller student networks, these architectures have now been applied across various knowledge learning objectives such as knowledge distillation, expansion, adaptation, and multi-task learning. Current research leveraging Teacher-Student architectures has successfully combined multiple knowledge-learning objectives with efficient, lightweight student networks. This distinct survey delves into the specifics of Teacher-Student architectures with multiple knowledge learning objectives and systematically explores knowledge construction and optimization processes, as well as analyzing various Teacher-Student architectures and learning schemes that produce robust and representative knowledge. Moreover, the paper summarizes and highlights the practical applications of Teacher-Student architectures across various purposes, such as classification, recognition, and generation, before exploring promising research directions, particularly on the design of Teacher-Student architectures, the quality of knowledge, and the theoretical studies of regression-based learning. With its in-depth analysis, this survey is poised to provide invaluable insights for industry practitioners and the academic community on the utilization of Teacher-Student architectures in multiple knowledge learning objectives. The paper is further organized into the following sections: introduction, Teacher-Student architectures for multiple knowledge learning objectives; applications of Teacher-Student architectures; and promising research directions. The paper concludes by examining the various Teacher-Student architectures used in multiple knowledge learning objectives, including knowledge distillation, knowledge expansion, knowledge adaptation, and multi-task learning, as well as presenting two new knowledge learning objectives: knowledge consolidation and knowledge stealing. The paper also explores the promising research directions on the design of Teacher-Student architectures, the quality of knowledge, and the theoretical studies of regression-based learning, and offers some final comments on the naming of Teacher-Student architectures in multiple knowledge learning objectives. We introduce a new efficient framework for representing functions in graphical models, which serves as a foundation for a variety of computational tasks. Our concise model then leverages this framework, specifically using deterministic finite state automata within a variable elimination approach known as Bucket Elimination. We dub this variant FABE, which we found significantly enhances Bucket Elimination by substantially reducing the computational time and memory usage. Our FABE approach compares favourably to the current state of the art methods, particularly recursive best-first and structured message passing for the most probable explanation, as well as CPLEX, GUROBI and toulbar2 for constrained optimisation, by achieving a 5 orders of magnitude improvement in our experiments following a widely established evaluation procedure. Our new model also provides readable representations that are notably more compact than the default representations, as demonstrated by our evaluation of 16 established graphical models. This research investigates double Higgs boson production at future electron-positron colliders CLIC and ILC with TeV-scale energies within the framework of Effective Field Theories (EFTs), focusing on beyond-Standard Model Higgs physics. Initially, we consider the Higgs Effective Field Theory (HEFT) and then compare the predictions with the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT). Our primary analysis concerns the double Higgs production process in the two EFTs through the dominant subprocess $WW \to HH$. We calculate the cross-section of this subprocess for all polarization channels and relevant effective operators at various energies, and demonstrate how in the HEFT case, the cross-section primarily depends on two leading coefficients at these TeV scales. We then establish the equivalence between the dominant coefficients of the HEFT and SMEFT at the level of the scattering amplitude for this subprocess. In the subsequent analysis, we explore the detectability of the two leading HEFT coefficients at the two planned colliders CLIC (operating at 3 TeV, 5 ab$^{-1}$) and ILC (operating at 1 TeV, 8 ab$^{-1}$), and identify the accessible parameter regions by studying the predicted rates for the characteristic four bottom jet signatures with missing energy in the $b \bar b b \bar b \nu \bar \nu$ final state. We find that at the ILC (CLIC) with 8 ab$^{-1}$ (5 ab$^{-1}$), the discovery reach extends to combinations of the two leading HEFT coefficients with magnitudes of order $10^{-5}$ ($10^{-4}$). We also compare the detection efficiencies of the two colliders for the same final state in the $b \bar b b \bar b \gamma \gamma$ channel, and investigate the potential of these experiments to distinguish between different EFTs, such as the HEFT and SMEFT. We conclude by outlining the prospects for detecting other less dominant subprocesses, and the possibilities of combining Higgs physics with other areas of rare processes at these colliders. We investigated the drag experienced by a long cylindrical solid moving through a layer of granular material, specifically polysterene and hydrogel grains, at various speeds and depths. The cylinder was oriented both perpendicular and parallel to its long axis as it moved, and we found that the drag it experienced differed significantly in the two orientations, a phenomenon we call anisotropy. This anisotropy varied greatly with the speed at which the cylinder was moved, its length compared to its width, and whether the grains it was moving through had high friction or little friction. Notably, the anisotropy increased more quickly in beds with low friction. Additionally, the drag experienced by the cylinder was found to be influenced more by its long axis than its ends. This phenomenon could be understood by studying the flow of sediment around the cylinder and estimating the drag experienced by its sides and flat ends. However, fully explaining the anisotropy of drag requires more complex flow models that take into account the grain's speed, the distance the grains move past each other, and the geometry of the cylinder. Nevertheless, our study shows that the drag experienced by a cylinder moving through granular material is governed by simple and complex flow models, and that fully explaining the anisotropy of drag requires both of these perspectives. Moreover, our study has implications for understanding the movement of long and narrow objects through sedimentary environments, and provides mathematical models that could be applied to such situations. Furthermore, our findings related to the drag experienced by cylinders moving through beds with low friction have been previously observed in other contexts, but have not been fully explained before. Lastly, our study has been conducted in a way that allows it to be compared with other similar experiments that have been carried out in the past.

Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles. Our findings were further validated by deriving the proportionality constant from the assumption of harmonic initial geometry and obtaining a centrality-independent value. Finally, our analysis demonstrated that the proportionality constant also holds for different collision energies and nuclei, varying only with transverse particle density. Consequently, we determined triangular flow's proportional relationship to the anisotropic initial geometry and overall multiplicity, making it a more reliable probe of the system's size than charge density. Our research was conducted using the multiphase transport model with initial geometry generated through Monte Carlo simulations from the AMPT model. Our findings were validated across a range of collisions, from 62.4 GeV Cu+Cu to 200 GeV Au+Au, and 39 GeV p+p. Our results were presented at the 21st International Conference on Nuclear Physics, 2019, in Bologna, Italy, as part of the "Physics with Heavy-Ion Collisions" session, within the "Nuclear Physics" category.

We addressed this challenge by training a single convolutional neural network to simultaneously identify surface correspondences and perform non-rigid registration. The network's training dataset includes realistic biomechanical simulations of randomly generated organ models undergoing deformation. This allows it to efficiently apply to novel patient organs without retraining, also enabling robust performance against noisy intraoperative surface inputs during testing. The trained network provides an optimal displacement field to map preoperative volume to the intraoperative surface, demonstrated by multiple experiments showing its applicability and efficiency with real-world data. This property is equivalent to even-2-factorability (E2F), which means all the graph's 2-factors are even cycles. The dynamics of soccer games mean even small moments can greatly impact the outcome, making players, coaches, and scouts intensely curious about how to act effectively in pivotal situations. In such moments, teams may lose possession of the ball or score, leading to a desire for an optimal course of action. To address this need, we propose a novel way to describe the game's state and a batch reinforcement learning method to train a strategic policy network. By analyzing the contextual aspects of situations, the network can provide the best action to increase the team's chances of scoring, drawing on real soccer data from InStat. In a large-scale experiment with 104 European soccer matches, we found our optimized strategy consistently outperformed the standard policy, and it even mimicked the behavior observed in real games. Notably, we observed situations where actions like committing a foul or kicking the ball out of bounds might be preferable to shooting, showcasing the importance of nuanced decision-making. By leveraging our model's insights, coaches can gain a deeper understanding of these situations and make more informed tactical decisions, such as deploying specific players in certain contexts. Furthermore, our methodology provides a framework for researching similar complex interactions in other sports, sports with similar dynamics, or even domains like military battles. The data and model code are available at https://github.com/soccer-reinforcement-learning/football.

High-resolution subsurface modeling via seismic imaging has the potential to be greatly improved with Full Waveform Inversion (FWI).  However, FWI can become trapped in local minima due to its nonlinear optimization nature. Two alternatives, Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (WRI) and Extended Source Waveform Inversion (ESI), have been proposed as methods to improve seismic imaging. Both of these methods relax the strict adherence to wave equation accuracy found in FWI and instead, WRI and ESI introduce non-physical source concepts that match observed data with synthetic data generated using extended sources. Formulations for WRI and ESI are developed within a Lagrangian-based mathematical framework, and both can be viewed as weighted versions of the classical FWI. Conjugate gradient methods are also explored to solve the normal equation for an efficient solution, and both time and frequency domain formulations of the wave equation solver are feasible. Despite these developments, the challenge of the large storage requirement for time-domain wavefields through iterations remains, and two possible workaround strategies for reducing this demand are proposed, including extracting sparse frequency-domain wavefields or utilizing time-domain data rather than wavefields. These innovations pave the way for an alternative seismic inversion method that prioritizes spatial accuracy over temporal accuracy, and suitable practical applications for such a method could be found in areas with complex structures and surface conditions.

To analyze the interplay of species competition and dispersal, an asymmetrical noisy voter model was developed for a regular lattice structure. The model allows one species to colonize nearest-neighbor sites, while another species can settle at any distance but is less successful in doing so. The model includes external noise, which can lead to random species swaps in the lattice. The combination of these dynamics results in various species competition outcomes, including the exclusion of one species, distinct population coexistence, or bistable coexistence dependent on the starting population ratio. The model shows that an abrupt transition occurs as immigration intensity surpasses a critical point, causing the irreversible decline of the species with shorter dispersal range due to a cusp catastrophe leading to half loop dynamics. The model further reveals that this catastrophe results in the inclusion of the opposing species in every instance, leading to its enhanced survival. The model also exhibits a regime with periodic oscillations in population sizes despite having an infinite number of possible initial conditions. The model's parameters were found to switch between different competition outcomes slowly over time, with the species coexistence window narrowing as external noise increases. The model further shows that the disruption of one species initially enhances the survival of the other, but this relationship reverses when the level of external noise surpasses a critical point, resulting in the decline of the dominant species and the survival of the weaker one. The model's results were validated by conducting additional experiments using a 1D lattice with a smaller size. The experiments showed that the model's outcomes are independent of lattice size, but the transition patterns are more complex in larger lattices. The model also exhibits species competition outcomes in a 2D square lattice, but the results are less rigorous due to the lattice's disordered nature. The model further analyzes the escape rate from the cusp catastrophe, which results in the exclusion of one species or the transition from half loop dynamics to the bistable regime. The model finds that the dispersal competition leads to the destruction of the cusp catastrophe in two dimensions, but the dynamics in this case are more complex due to the diversity of possible situations in a 2D square lattice. The model further reveals that the dispersal competition results in the survival of the weaker species in three dimensions, but the dynamics in this case are more complex due to the diversity of possible situations in a 3D cube lattice. The model also analyzes the effects of changes in migration and birth death rates on species competition outcomes in all lattice structures. This research focuses on an integrated data and energy transmission network, which incorporates D2D communication. This hybrid network allows a central hub to transfer data to those in need and supply power to those who require it. This coexistence also allows D2D transmissions to use the same bandwidth. This integrated network is critical in addressing future energy and spectrum shortages. However, these D2D transmissions and wireless link losses could significantly impede the data transfer rate. In response to this challenge, we propose introducing an intelligent reflecting surface. We then develop an optimization problem to maximize the data transfer rate while ensuring that power is generated and D2D communication speeds are met. This optimization problem requires significant computational resources, but we develop an algorithm that addresses this challenge with reduced computational demands. Finally, simulations confirm the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm. This research also explores key variations of the integrated network, which includes varying D2D communication distances and the number of D2D users. This research was previously published in the IEEE International Conference on Communications (ICC) in 2021 under the title "Integrated Data and Energy Transmission Network with D2D Communications". This revised version includes an updated introduction and background information. Additionally, this version includes an analysis of the baseline scenario, an exploration of an energy harvesting D2D transmission network, and an examination of a scenario with varying D2D transmission distances. We derive new conclusions regarding the additive Galois module properties of specific wildly ramified finite non-abelian extensions of Q. Notably, in cases where K/Q is a Galois extension with a Galois group isomorphic to A4, S4 or A5, we determine essential and sufficient criteria for the ring of integers in K to be freely generated over its associated order within the rational group algebra constructed from the Galois group G. Conversely, we establish that for each of these three groups, there exist infinitely many Galois extensions with a rational G-algebra structure, thereby providing examples of non-abelian extensions with specific module properties. However, even when restricted to single passes through the input, some functions in these models can still be undecidable by Turing machines with infinite input, despite being defined by finite-state machines. To address this issue, a new decision-making approach is proposed for determining whether a specific function is computable and if so, to create a corresponding Turing machine. 

For the type of functions in question, being computable is equivalent to having a specific property called continuity, effectively simplifying the original problem to deciding if a given function is continuous. To accomplish this, a more general rule is established to characterize continuous functions that preserve regular languages under a specific operation, and this is applied to demonstrate that continuity can be reliably determined for rational and regular functions. Furthermore, this decision-making approach is efficient and takes only $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$, a previously known but higher $\mathsf{PTime}$ requirement.

The paper addresses the problem of bias in vector magnetic field maps, particularly in estimating the component perpendicular to the line-of-sight, Bperp. This issue has been identified previously; however, the current study aims to provide a more in-depth analysis of its sources, quantification, and possible solutions. Initially, the authors establish precise metrics to assess Bperp bias, accounting for both local and native components. Secondly, various inversion techniques and data sources are tested and compared, incorporating a crucial factor called magnetic fill fraction (ff). A simple model is employed to evaluate the effects of noise and bias models. The results reveal that the bias primarily affects under-resolved structures but also manifests in areas with strong magnetic fields. Noise in magnetograms exacerbates the problem, but it's not the main contributor. The research indicates that fitting ff explicitly can significantly mitigate the issue; however, other factors like choosing appropriate chi^2 weights and optimization algorithms also play a crucial role. Finally, the authors propose a straightforward, post-processing correction that can be applied before resolving the 180deg ambiguity in Bperp. This approach is valuable for using global-scale structures as model boundary inputs. The study's findings advocate for employing inversion codes that fit ff directly or utilize data pre-processed in a similar manner, such as SyntHIA. The research was conducted using the Optimization Code (OC) and the Metropolis-Helbig model but the findings are applicable to other inversion and bias models. The authors' analysis provides a framework for evaluating and improving vector magnetic field map inference techniques. The work presented is relevant to solar research and has broader implications for magnetometric inference techniques in general. A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem. Moreover, this complex-valued network can be trained end-to-end, thereby facilitating the optimal path transformation through stochastic reinforcement learning. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method by successfully simulating a highly challenging case of finite-temperature Monte Carlo simulations for a one-dimensional Hubbard model with a severe sign problem. Our complex-valued network achieves a precision of 99.9\% in determining the ground-state energy per site for this model. Furthermore, we show that this architecture can be combined with multilayer flow networks, offering a route to efficiently solve polarizable continuous-time Monte Carlo simulations. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/AyaneAnai/Complex_NN_CTMCS.

By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-augmentation method known as ReCross, which employs unlabeled samples to selectively draw from existing data, fine-tune the model for better performance.
The proposed method seamlessly integrates both high-efficiency dense retrieval and a more effective pair-wise re-ranking process to produce outstanding results, surpassing non-retrieval methods and alternative baselines in our experiments. ReCross delivers remarkable performance in multiple evaluation metrics across diverse datasets and taxonomic categories, confirming the versatility and effectiveness of the proposed approach. The associated code and model are available for public use.

The results of our experiments, conducted using MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning, show significant improvements over the conventional grid search method. The paper addresses existing challenges and potential research directions in the field, and provides an open-source code for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning. The code is available at https://github.com/HongSeokYou/DP-HyperParameterTuning. For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of involutions within W, mirroring Ragnarsson and Tenner's previous work. By applying discrete Morse theory, we identify the homotopy type of this boolean complex for a significant subset of Coxeter groups, including finite groups, revealing that its homotopy type is equivalent to that of a collection of spheres with dimension |S|-1. Moreover, we derive straightforward, recursive formulas to compute the number of spheres within this collection. Additionally, we derive connections between these boolean complexes and the underlying geometry of W, incorporating properties such as the group's structure, specific permutation groups, and the boolean complexes defined by graph-theoretic representations. Specifically, we examine the case of W being a finite permutation group, determining that its boolean complex consists of a single sphere with a dimension equal to the number of elements in S. Furthermore, we establish an analogous result for the boolean complex associated with the symmetric group S_n, whose dimension is (n-1). Lastly, we offer a statistical analysis of the boolean complex associated with the Coxeter group S_n, demonstrating that its number, encompassing all possible spheres, can be represented as the product of two factors: the number of elements in S, and the coefficient associated with each dimension, given by a descending binomial coefficient. Lastly, we include an appendix detailing the boolean complexes defined by the graph-theoretic representation of the Coxeter group B_n, revealing that they are equivalent to those defined by the permutation group S_n.

To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Subsequently, we developed and evaluated machine learning models, discovering that decision trees effectively forecast the peak coefficient and linear regression accurately predicts the attenuation coefficient. Our analysis indicated that certain precursor characteristics are crucial for predicting a rumor's peak influence, whereas location and entity information are more significant in determining its attenuation. A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been discovered by examining extragalactic planetary nebulae, specifically due to their nearly universal brightness pattern. Determining the precise distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae analysis depends on collecting comprehensive data sets, and the observed frequency of these nebulae directly correlates with the galaxies' overall mass. Therefore, researchers must either utilize wide-field observations or focus on the central areas of galaxies. By focusing on the central areas, a comprehensive study has been conducted of the planetary nebulae residing within early-type galaxies located within the Fornax cluster using spectroscopic observations taken from the VLT/MUSE data collection from the Fornax3D survey. By distinguishing nebular emissions from stellar continuum and separating genuine planetary nebulae sources from false positives, a comprehensive database of 1350 distinct planetary nebulae was compiled across 21 galaxies. Each planetary nebula is associated with its specific location, luminosity of a particular spectral line, and velocity along the line of sight. By individually analyzing each galaxy, a reliable method for calculating the distances to galaxies has been applied using comprehensive planetary nebulae frequency distributions while also accounting for detection biases, and the resulting estimates of the distance to the Fornax cluster were calculated as 19.86 megaparsecs with an associated margin of error. Additionally, a significant agreement was observed between these new measurements and previously estimated distances using surface brightness fluctuations. The accuracy of the planned $4\pi$ steradian coverage planetary nebulae searches for the ATLAS3D gallery of galaxies is predicted to yield similar levels of precision in distance estimation. The comprehensive data set of planetary nebulae frequencies and individual object records presented here will serve as valuable resources for further studying the formation and physical properties of galaxy populations. Every day, hospitals around the world gather vast amounts of physiological data from their patients, leading to an escalating interest in conducting statistical analyses to provide better medical diagnoses. These analyses involve complex computations on significant datasets, necessitating high-performance data processing systems that can balance efficiency and simplicity. To address the limitations of existing data processing solutions, we present \emph{LifeStream}, a robust stream processing engine specifically designed to handle physiological data efficiently. LifeStream optimizes performance while providing intuitive temporal query language support, thus striking a balance between ease of programming and computational speed. Furthermore, LifeStream exhibits superior performance, outperforming other leading stream processing engines and hand-tuned numerical libraries by up to $7.5\times$ and $3.2\times$ respectively, on realistic datasets and workload simulations. With its ease of use, efficiency, and scalability, LifeStream is an suitable platform for medical researchers and clinicians to conduct time-series analytical studies on patient data. The system's source code is available at \url{https://github.com/LifeStreamProject/LifeStream}.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant. To demonstrate this, we employ a simple yet effective strategy called OptLF, leveraging a bare minimum of additional computational resources to achieve satisfactory results. Our experiments with multiple networks, including ResNets and efficient NetLfts, showcase the versatility of our approach, which can be applied to various scenarios, including cloud-based remote computation networks, where a centralized entity hosts the network and conducts computations on behalf of individual clients. Our study highlights the significance of loss function optimization for real-world applications, where networks often operate in a cloud-based setting, as seen in anti-drone systems, intelligent surveillance systems, and certain medical imaging contexts. Our findings also open up new research directions, as evident in the accompanying discussion. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghrasoul/EvalLoss.

To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic susceptibility in nematic and chiral superconducting states using the Ginzburg-Landau formalism near its critical temperature. A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response to the transverse component of an applied magnetic field, which can result in a paramagnetic response. Moreover, the topology of the Fermi surface exerts a substantial influence on magnetic susceptibility, with a specific Lifshitz transition inducing a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase and leading to the divergence of magnetic susceptibility at this transition point. Notably, the interplay between electron-electron interaction and competing phases of superconductivity is investigated, with results showing that the driving force behind a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase can be the presence of electron-electron interaction in the immediate vicinity of the transition. A comparison with existing experimental data is also presented in this analysis. The importance of incorporating spin polarization into the analysis of this system is emphasized, with results showing that the omission of spin polarization can lead to the incorrect prediction of the divergence of the anomalous Hall conductivity in this system. A discussion on the relevance of this analysis to other materials exhibiting spin-triplet nematic superconductivity is also provided in this paper. The computational methodology used in this analysis is based on the Ginzburg-Landau formalism and the tight-binding Hamiltonian method, with results showing that the Ginzburg-Landau formalism yields reliable results when the clean-limit conditions are met, while the tight-binding Hamiltonian method is capable of analyzing more complex situations involving the disorder of dopants and Lifshitz transitions in the Fermi surface. Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly resistant to various channel disturbances, such as phase and Doppler shift. Its basic structure makes its implementation uncomplicated, involving the product of a received baseband signal and a time-reversed version of one symbol duration. Nevertheless, it experiences reduced signal-to-noise ratio compared to coherent detection methods. In this research, the performance of conventional differential detection is enhanced through increased delay periods. By accounting for $K$ symbol delays, the trellis structure and relevant branch and cumulative metrics are derived, resulting in an optimized criterion for $K$. This criterion is based on the minimum Euclidean distance between differential signals, ultimately facilitating the selection of ideal delay periods for popular CPM formats through simulated error rates verification. In particular, the proposed approach is applied to three widely used CPM formats: MSK, GMSK, and MINSEK, yielding favorable outcomes. In these cases, the optimal delay periods are found to be 5, 9, and 11 symbols, respectively. In general, the proposed method provides a straightforward yet reliable way of manually determining desirable delay periods for other CPM formats. In addition, this research investigates the relationship between signal-to-noise ratio and delay period, revealing that its characteristic curve shares the same interval-based pattern as its coherent detection counterpart. In such a scenario, standard coherent different detection can be employed as a substitute, allowing for the selection of an appropriate coherent detection scheme, following which the corresponding delayed conventional differential detection can be readily determined. Portfolio optimization is a critical application in Finance, yet its computational intricacies compel financial institutions to resort to simplified methods that require considerable time. By leveraging the Lagrange multiplier method, the mean-variance portfolio optimization issue can be formulated into a set of linear equations and potentially take advantage of the accelerated performance offered by the HHL quantum algorithm. Nevertheless, certain HHL components are not well-suited for operation on Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum hardware. This research introduces NISQ-HHL, the first hybrid rendition of HHL that is capable of supporting end-to-end execution of compact-scale portfolio-optimization tasks on NISQ devices. NISQ-HHL enhances the hybrid HHL variation with newly available quantum-hardware capabilities, encompassing mid-circuit measurement, qubit reinitialization and reutilization, and Quantum Conditional Logic. Moreover, NISQ-HHL integrates an enhanced Phase Estimation executed on actual hardware, namely the trapped-ion Quantinuum System Model H1-1, alongside a novel approach to determine the optimal duration of Hamiltonian simulation. This research centers on portfolio optimization but presents solutions applicable to any problem addressed via HHL within the Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum era. The NISQ-HHL code is publicly accessible on GitHub at the following location: https://github.com/QuantumFinance/NISQHHL.

To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models and enable them to handle a large amount of unpaired text data through multi-modal training, it's essential to address two challenges: synchronizing the sampling rates of speech and language features and ensuring that the learned representations from both encoders are consistent. This paper introduces a novel bidirectional attention mechanism that combines the learning of both the ASR and text encoders using a multi-modal learning method. This attention mechanism facilitates the exchange of sampling rates, effectively allowing the quality of transformed features to be measured in an alternative space. This leads to speech representations being enriched with more linguistic information, while the text representations are made more similar to speech, enabling ASR models to effectively leverage unpaired text data for pretraining. Experimental evaluations on the Librispeech corpus reveal a significant 6.15% reduction in word error rate when only paired data is used and up to 9.23% when additional unpaired text data is applied. This approach also surpasses the performance of E2E ASR models trained with hidden states from a pre-trained language model. The code for this project is available at github.com/lingcat/speech-text-modal.

The critical voltage of these nanowires is observed to be tunable using an adjacent gate electrode and varies significantly in response to applied voltage, aligning with expected results of quantum interference but exhibiting unanticipated periodic variations. The magnitude of these periodic variations far exceeds predictions based on capacitance alone and presents a discrepancy in understanding this phenomenon, especially after observing sudden period shifts during measurements. The possibility of attributing the behavior to granular Josephson junctions within the nanowires is also considered, offering an alternative explanation for the findings. The observed effects also prompt the use of a new characterization method involving modulation of the gate voltage to analyze the nanowires' properties. Our proposed approach tackles the challenge of novel view video prediction, taking input from multiple viewpoints. Unlike existing research that relies on narrow angle variations, our network can generate videos from significantly wider angles, up to 45 degrees, without the need for prior knowledge. By processing only RGB frames, we've developed a two-component representation, combining local and global features that enables novel view prediction. Our model achieves remarkable results on real-world datasets NTU-RGB+D and CMU Panoptic, surpassing the state-of-the-art in novel view video prediction, demonstrating significant gains in SSIM, PSNR, and FVD scores of 26.1%, 13.6%, and 60% respectively, without the use of prior views. Our code is now available on GitHub at https://github.com/abhinav97/NovelViewVideoPrediction.

Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as various ventilation methods, temperature-driven buoyancy effects, and surface deposition of aerosols. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we used numerical models of unsteady airflow to analyze and visualize virus-laden aerosol transport. In comparing our detailed model to a widely accepted 'well mixed' model, notable discrepancies in the distribution of aerosol particles became evident, with implications for our understanding of the spread of airborne pathogens. Furthermore, the differences identified in our study are expected to be relevant to a broader range of enclosed settings beyond urban buses. In considering the practical applications of our findings, we believe there are arguments both for and against the use of a 'well mixed' model by public health officials. On one hand, using such a model could lead to overestimation of the speed of transmission, potentially resulting in incorrect policy decisions, whereas on the other hand, it may still provide a useful, easier-to-implement alternative for guiding critical decisions, given the complex nature of the 'full resolved' model. Hence, our study emphasizes the need for further research into the airflow dynamics of confined environments, with additional analysis of various noxious airborne pathogens conducted using both 'full resolved' and 'well mixed' models. This approach will help in assessing the differences in transmission rates predicted by these models, with the ultimate goal of developing more effective strategies for preventing the spread of such pathogens. The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves a rise in Spin-Orbit Coupling near a strong spin-orbit material's interface with an adjacent layer. In the study presented here, magnetoelectrical transport, specifically magnetoresistance and the anomalous Hall effect, were investigated in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers in search of Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect and an analysis of its origin. Findings suggest that very thin Cobalt layers exhibit increased Spontaneous Magnetic Anisotropy of Resistivity and Anomalous Hall Resistivity. An examination of Anomalous Hall Resisitivity revealed that the Bismuth layers modify the Hall effect's scattering mechanism to the extrinsic skew-scattering type, suggesting that the spin-orbit proximity effect could result from elastic scattering of Cobalt's free carriers by Bismuth sites at the interface. In summary, this research on Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers reveals that the spin-orbit proximity effect can arise from elastic scattering of carriers by the Bismuth sites at the interface, or directly from the intrinsic properties of the interface, depending on the preparation method. Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches have primarily focused on utilizing training datasets similar to their test data, neglecting performance evaluation for new acquisitions outside of their distribution. We developed a novel neural network framework that incorporates the physics underlying the PET imaging process and estimates output uncertainty to address these limitations. This new uncertainty-aware neural network framework can utilize low-dose PET scans and accompanying MRI data to generate high-quality PET images at standard doses, thus enhancing robustness when processing out-of-distribution data, such as various forms of OOD PET-MRI acquisitions. Experimental results confirm the advantages of this model in enhancing PET images both quantitatively and qualitatively in various settings. The code is available at https://github.com/yongchunyang/PMNet.

A linguistic analysis known as centering theory (CT) explains how coherence in conversations emerges from the connections between successive statements. This paper explores the link between CT and advanced computer systems that identify relationships within a text. By developing specific metrics and a search-based method, the study examines if modern computer systems that recognize connections within a text align with the principles of CT. The analysis indicates a correlation between the systems' ability to recognize connections and their ability to model the coherence of the text, but also reveals that these computer systems are not necessarily improved by considering the ideas underlying CT. Furthermore, the study finds that these computer systems already incorporate the coherence information required to recognize connections within the text, making CT's contribution limited. Additionally, the study discusses aspects that influence connections within the text but are not accounted for by CT, including the systems' knowledge and their tendency to favor more recent statements. By incorporating these elements, the study presents a revised version of CT and shows that it better captures the connections within the text compared to the original CT. The revised version of CT also provides insights into the structure of the texts that the systems find most coherent. The study concludes by analyzing the different versions of CT and identifying which aspects are relevant for evaluating the coherence of texts and identifying relationships within the text. The revised version of CT outperforms the original version of CT and provides the most accurate results among the versions tested, with significant improvements when evaluating the connections within the text, but only minor changes when evaluating the relationships within the text. The study ends by discussing the implications of these findings for future developments in computer systems that identify relationships within a text, with opportunities to explore the ideas underlying CT and incorporate elements that influence connections within the text. The study also presents a curated dataset of 500 texts with corresponding CT annotations, available for public use. The results reported in this paper were obtained using a particular computer system, with 92% accuracy when recognizing connections within the text, but the study finds that the majority of the current computer systems would yield similar results. The paper ends by presenting a hypothetical scenario in which future developments in computer systems that identify relationships within a text, incorporating the ideas underlying CT, could lead to a better comprehension of coherence in conversations, with the possibility of evaluating the coherence of the texts and identifying relationships within the text using the revised version of CT, and analyzing the different versions of CT to determine which aspects are relevant for this task. Recently, WiFi has become the primary method for locating individuals or devices within indoor settings. To facilitate this process, WiFi fingerprinting, a technique where reference measurements with known locations are collected and analyzed, has become a standard approach in positioning methods and algorithms discussed in academic literature. However, measuring spatial distances between these collected data sets, also known as WiFi fingerprints, relies heavily on the choice of signal distance metric employed to map signal intensity to geographical distance. To address this issue, the researchers proposed using machine learning to enhance the estimation of geospatial distances between these data sets. This research analyzed 13 diverse datasets from various open sources in order to create a universally applicable model suitable for a wide range of indoor environments. The novel approach developed extracted meaningful data features from a set of conventional signal distance metrics using feature selection and genetic algorithms. To demonstrate the versatility of this approach, models were tested on previously unused datasets from the training and validation stages. Furthermore, a comparative analysis was conducted among different machine learning algorithms utilizing a wide range of evaluation metrics, including their scalability to accommodate diverse real-world datasets. The data sets used in this research included university campuses, offices, shopping malls, museums, hotels, airports, sports centers, schools, and libraries among others, totaling over 39,000 distinct WiFi fingerprint data sets. The most promising model, a decision tree, was found to be particularly effective in predicting accurate distances between these data sets and is readily applicable to various real-world scenarios with minimal adjustment. The novel approach developed in this research is suitable for a wide range of indoor environments and is universally applicable to a wide range of scenarios with minimal adjustment, as demonstrated by the data presented in this paper. The algorithm developed has been made available online for further development and modification by interested researchers. The research also highlights various techniques that can be employed to improve the accuracy of machine learning-based distance estimation in different real-world scenarios. The novel approach developed in this research provides a framework for modifying and further developing machine learning-based distance estimation algorithms for different real-world scenarios, as demonstrated by the data presented in this paper. The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling patterns and recirculation schemes on beam and RF system interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This paper delves deeper into this subject by examining how filling patterns influence beam breakup instability and explores opportunities to optimize design for reduced instability effects. A theoretical beam-RF interaction model along with numerical modeling demonstrates that threshold currents can differ by 2-4 factors or even more, depending on machine design parameters. Consequently, carefully selecting filling patterns can delay the onset of beam breakup, enhancing the potential applications of future energy recovery linacs. Furthermore, this work identifies critical parameters including gap distribution, space-holding, and beam loss restriction that must be considered in designing stable and efficient energy recovery linacs. To extend the BFKL equation to NNLL accuracy, the one-loop CEV for two gluons with low rapidity ordering must be known. In this work, the dispersive part of a one-loop six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory was calculated under a NMRK kinematic limit and shown to be composed of a two-gluon CEV, allowing extraction of the latter for all helicity configurations. Although this calculation was constrained to the NMRK limit, the resulting two-gluon CEV exhibits significant complexity in both color and kinematic dependence, mirroring characteristics found in general six-gluon amplitude configurations. In such scenarios, six-gluon amplitude functions can be expressed using impact factors, trajectories, CEVs for single-emission processes, and a residual component defined by conformally invariant cross ratios that characterise six-gluon amplitudes in N=4 SYM theory. As expected, under a stricter MRK kinematic limit, the two-gluon CEV can be decomposed into a product of two single-emission CEVs. In both limits, the two-gluon CEV exhibits helicity non-conservation, with coefficients that match known results. Furthermore, under the MRK limit, six-gluon amplitude functions in N=4 SYM theory are well-defined and depend on impact factors, trajectories, single-emission CEVs, and cross ratios that characterise six-gluon amplitudes in N=4 SYM theory. As a byproduct, this work also facilitates extraction of a particular six-gluon amplitude function in QCD, albeit under the same MRK kinematic limit. In both theories, this amplitude function shares the same form as a six-gluon amplitude function in N=4 SYM theory, but with different cross ratio coefficients that can be determined using unitarity methods. This finds additional support from a dual-grassmann-GL(6) matrix decomposition approach, which directly relates the six-gluon amplitude function to a particular BPS operator in N=4 SYM theory and implies its dependence on cross ratio coefficients as characterising six-gluon amplitudes in N=4 SYM theory. This perspective also allows interpretation of the six-gluon amplitude function as a sum over contributions from an array of two-gluon CEVs, each associated with a distinct BPS operator in N=4 SYM theory. This viewpoint further extends to seven-gluon amplitude configurations in N=4 SYM

Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush properties have provided valuable insights into the behavior of surface-grafted polymers in various scenarios. However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a zone devoid of free chain ends and demands a revised theoretical analysis. Although the 'end exclusion zone' concept has been successfully incorporated into models for cylindrical and spherical surfaces, its implications for curved surfaces with varied geometries have yet to be explored. In this study, we introduce a revised strong-stretching theory that applies to molten polymer brushes on curved surfaces of any complexity, identifying distinct regimes that give rise to end exclusion zones - including those with positive curvature and negative Gaussian curvature. By numerically solving the strong-stretching brush equations, we predict how the size of the end exclusion zone, chain end distribution, chain polarization, and free energy of stretching change with mean and Gaussian curvatures, offering a detailed understanding of how surface curvature affects brush geometry and free energy calculations. This comprehensive knowledge can be utilized to simulate a broad range of brush geometries encountered in the assembly of block copolymer melts. Moreover, our findings agree with previous research on surfaces with simple curvatures and accurately describe the behavior of brushes on surfaces with complex curvatures, making them applicable to a wide range of block copolymer morphology scenarios. The 'end exclusion zone' concept and associated theoretical predictions can be experimentally verified using advanced characterization techniques such as high-resolution transmission electron microscopy. The end exclusion zone phenomenon also offers valuable insights into brush geometry at equilibrium, providing a means to measure surface curvature and nanoscale structural details of block copolymer interfaces. A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph. It turns out this property is equivalent to a graph being k-connected. Also we find the beta_k of trees, show it equals the maximum node degree in a star graph, and determine that a tree with n nodes has a metric dimension of at most 2 for distances of up to sqrt(n-1). Furthermore we find that an arbitrary graph's metric dimension is equal to the maximum node degree of any subgraph, and that determining this property is NP-hard. Lastly we discuss some implications of this property for certain processes that generate random samples of vertices. This version of metric dimension may also be relevant to other fields where it is known by other names, such as "minimum dominating set" or "maximum independent set" where the distance between points is given by a non-Euclidean norm. One such example is shown here where a "Jaccard dimension" of genetic data is equivalent to a particular complexity metric that can be difficult to calculate but is crucial for interpreting the results of certain genetic analyses. This is particularly true for techniques like MIRA, GESEL, and MPA, and provides a simple and efficient alternative or companion test that can be based on a simpler metric such as the number of overlapping markers between samples. Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. The machine learning-based method enhanced the image quality compared to standard techniques, particularly in replicating complex diffuse emissions from the galactic plane. These models can simplify image analysis by sidestepping assumptions about emission patterns, yet they also struggle with temporally varying sources, like blazars, which change significantly over a year. Despite this limitation, this approach shows promise for automatically identifying these sources and detecting transient phenomena and giant structures often missed in focused observations. To optimize the algorithms for better handling of temporally Varying sources, the team developed a system that prioritizes sources differently based on their observed brightness, and tested this method on a renowned gamma-ray source, the Large Magellanic Cloud. This framework and associated code are available online. This research was conducted in partnership with the Fermi Science Support Center and the Gammapy development team.

Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving a range of combinatorial optimization problems by employing a basic model where multiple agents take sequential actions. The model stipulates that each agent chooses their optimal action based on the actions taken by previous agents in the predetermined order. We aim to identify action sequences that maximize overall value for all agents involved. We establish theoretical bounds on achievable social welfare when employing a query-based approach and find that this results in a marginally improved approximation of optimal social welfare when considering a general scenario. However, when combinatorial optimization domains are in question, we demonstrate the ability to obtain high-quality approximations, achieving a $2$-approximation when applying it to specific optimization tasks including graph matching, arborescence in directed graphs, and Boolean satisfiability. We also examine issues of honesty and provide ways in which some of our solutions can be implemented fairly with incentives based on payment schemes such as the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves method. We propose and evaluate a new metric, the price of serial dictatorship, offering a quantitative indicator of the efficacy of combinatorial optimization solutions obtained via action sequences. We present a comprehensive review of existing and our own solutions, analyzing the productivity of different action sequences and validating our metrics by comparing the effectiveness of various combinations of agents in various scenarios. We conclude by outlining potential applications of this research to static and dynamic scenarios, as well as its connection to related topics including mechanism design, multi-agent optimization, and graph theory. We make available our own-created Python code for refereeing purposes, available at https://github.com/optimus21/SDDMO. In addition, we provide a conference presentation at CP2023 available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UyvzG6s64gA. We offer solutions to the described problems and challenging tasks, including but not limited to the following: (1) the problem of finding a perfect matching in a bipartite graph, (2) the arborescence problem in directed graphs, (3) the Boolean satisfiability problem, (4) the bin-packing problem, (5) the clustering problem, (6) the scheduling problem, and (7) the transportation problem in a grid. We hope this work might serve as a foundation for both theoretical and practical ongoing and future research in this domain. We also invite interested researchers to collaborate with us.
