Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as skewing) transformations, then we outline general robustness validation strategies for all categories. Additionally, we design unique validation protocols tailored to a variety of specific transformation scenarios. Experimental results on multiple frequent three-dimensional transformations demonstrate the exceptional performance of TPC surpassing current standards with notable improvements. As an example, our method achieves significant enhancement in validated accuracy when dealing with twisting transformation along the z-axis (within a 20-degree range) from 20.3% to 83.8%. All code and models are available for use at https://github.com/Qianhewu/Point-Cloud-Smoothing.

Within the RPA framework, the Jost function method has been enhanced to detect complex RPA eigenenergies in the complex energy plane. By applying this method, the RPA poles that characterize excited states such as $^{16}$O's electric dipole giant resonance were located within the complex energy plane with great success. Contrary to traditional views, research has revealed that the $^{16}$O electric dipole giant resonance, which has historically been understood as a solitary and broad resonance, actually consists of multiple poles with distinct widths, origins, residual interaction responses, and distinct densities of fluctuation components within the RPA framework. These findings with the Jost function method have been compared to the results obtained from the complex energy surface or the pole map in the complex energy plane obtained using the complex scaling method. Although both methods yielded the same overall understanding of $^{16}$O's RPA poles, they revealed distinct aspects of the same phenomenon. The Jost function method provides a more in-depth analysis of the resonant states, residual interaction responses, and the densities of fluctuation components that form the giant resonance. On the other hand, the complex scaling method offers a broader perspective of the giant resonance, encompassing its overall distribution in the complex energy plane. By applying both methods, researchers have gained a more comprehensive and detailed understanding of $^{16}$O's RPA poles, including the complex eigenenergies of the electric dipole giant resonance. On the theoretical side, the analysis of $^{16}$O's RPA poles has also led to the discovery of a previously unreported positive charge state RPA pole at an energy of approximately 20 MeV, in addition to the well-known electric dipole giant resonance at 16.1 MeV, the 4$^{\rm th}$ giant resonance at 24 MeV, the 2$^{\rm nd}$ monopole giant resonance at 20 MeV, and the 1$^{\rm st}$ isoscalar giant resonance at 80 MeV, among others. Furthermore, this has allowed for an explicit identification of the 4$^{\rm th}$ giant resonance as a dense and narrow resonance that was initially overlooked. Moreover, both methods have demonstrated that the widths of the RPA poles are influenced by the densities of the fluctuation components within the RPA framework, rather than simply being determined by the absorption widths. This has also been confirmed by means of the complex scaling method or the analysis of the RPA poles' pole maps

Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizes the Koopman operator to handle nonlinear relationships, thus extending the approach to a broad spectrum of applications. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through clustering of a linear system, the non-linear 39-bus transmission network, and variables derived from atmospheric data in the Amazon rainforest. This work's contribution is reflected in its utilization of operational tools for community detection in complex systems, encompassing a straightforward yet effective algorithm, and its open-source code is available at https://github.com/Apidan/InfluenceClustering.

Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient adversarial training by reducing noise but also enable a fully differentiable training process. Experimental evaluations on various text generation datasets demonstrate improved performance, particularly in terms of sequence-level metrics like BLEU scores. Moreover, our model surpasses existing GAN-based baselines in both the MEMEPOCETT and MMIM frameworks, setting a new standard for text generation using GANs. The code for SparseGAN is available at https://github.com/ghrua/SparseGAN.

The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another, a concept known as interstellar panspermia, has its roots in the distant past, but the challenge remains of being able to observe this theory in action. To tackle this issue, a mathematical model is developed which takes into consideration various factors including how long microbial life forms can survive, the speed of stars dispersing, and how ejected material scatters across space, all to assess the likelihood of discovering evidence for interstellar panspermia. By examining statistical relationships between pairs of life-bearing planetary systems, a potential indicator of interstellar panspermia emerges under certain astrophysical conditions. Estimates for various environments suggest that clusters of open and globular stars represent the most suitable subjects for investigating the validity of interstellar panspermia. Specifically, the open star cluster NGC 6704 and the globular cluster Omega Centauri are identified as particularly promising case studies. To succeed, researchers would need multiple pairs of stars carrying life within these clusters, a scenario that can be guided by determining the optimal criteria for pair formation breakdown based on factors like orbital periods and spectral analysis of star movements and velocities. Although the technical difficulties of achieving this are significant, detecting interstellar panspermia in these star clusters could provide a groundbreaking finding, offering insights into how life spreads across the galaxy. Furthermore, a related concept, known as planetary biosferic persistence, is introduced as a separate area of investigation that can yield valuable insights into the spread of life and the stability of planetary ecosystems. Although interstellar panspermia remains purely theoretical, detecting it remains a tangible goal within the realm of astrophysics. To move forward, a collaborative effort is required from biologists, astronomers, and planetary scientists to develop a comprehensive understanding of this phenomenon and the life forms it contains. Ultimately, successful detection of interstellar panspermia would mark a major achievement in the search for life beyond the planet Earth.

Another significant focus of wildlife research involves calculating population size and density.  New spatial capture-recapture models can achieve this goal using individual encounter histories combined with location information from captures.  These models incorporate encounter probability functions connected to resource selection functions.  However, no previous studies have explored combining capture-recapture and resource selection data to estimate space usage, resource selection, and population density simultaneously.  We present a statistical method that integrates capture data from various sources with telemetry data to model these components jointly and provides a likelihood-based estimation framework to estimate the SCR and RSF model parameters at once.  This method results in enhanced precision when estimating population density and standard capture-recapture model parameters.  Notably, our study reveals that capture-recapture models alone can infer parameters for resource selection functions, enabling the exclusive use of capture data to investigate space usage, albeit with lower precision.  Nonetheless, using telemetry data yields superior precision.  We discovered that models employing standard encounter probability models can provide biased estimates of density when animals' spatial behavior correlates with environmental variables, which necessitates consideration of space usage in population density estimations through capture-recapture methods.  Ultimately, our research delivers capture-recapture-specific models, including a novel approach using mark-resight data, along with integrated capture-recapture and resource selection models that can be applied to diverse ecological scenarios.  We also provide R code to facilitate implementation of these models.  Our analysis involves modeling the spatial distribution of encounters, marks, and captures in relation to environmental variables, which yields a capture-recapture-based estimate of resource selection functions and enables comparison of space usage and resource selection among different groups.  Our study illustrates the statistical models' applicability to tortoise data and marks tree-ring growth patterns in relation to environmental variables, which can be useful for managing forestry. To overcome this challenge, we present a method for examining the dynamics of Kuramoto oscillators within multilayer networks by applying a joint matrix representation. This technique provides a compact representation of the multilayer system that maintains equivalent dynamics. As a result, we can determine solutions for the reduced system and then extend them to the multilayer network. Furthermore, we can investigate the stability of these solutions by analyzing the reduced system and obtaining insights into the multilayer system's Jacobian. Our method is adaptable to different interlayer node connections. Ultimately, our research enables the exploration of multilayer networks through simplified representations, facilitating a deeper understanding of the complex dynamics underlying these systems. Given a linear differential operator, determining its generating compatibility conditions, an operator with which it is invariant when applied to a given differential equation, is known as the direct problem. This process yields successive first-order operators for an n-dimensional manifold. The converse, an inverse problem, is to find the original differential operator when one of these compatibility operators is known. The compatibility operator can be parameterized by the original differential operator only if it defines a torsion-free differential module. The parametrization is minimal when this differential module has a vanishing differential rank. Notably, attempts to parameterize the Cauchy stress operator have been a subject of study for renowned scientists such as G.B. Airy, J.C. Maxwell, and A. Einstein. This work identifies a widespread misconception among them, mistakenly using the Einstein operator and confusing it with the Cauchy operator and the $div$ operator induced from the Bianchi operator. As an interesting aside, determining whether Einstein was aware of previous work is a historical puzzle. This study also clarifies misinterpretations of his words in "Mein Leben" by L. Földi. Furthermore, a discussion on the (mis)use of the term "symmetric" in tensor theory during the 19th and early 20th centuries is presented. The widespread ignorance of the differential module's role in defining the Cauchy operator correctly led to the notorious "Einstein's error" in his general relativity theory. This led to a temporary correction by him as reported in "Zeitschrift für Physik" Volume 17, but was later mistakenly considered a correction to the Bianchi identity rather than the Cauchy operator. As a result, this correction has been misinterpreted and misunderstood by later generations. Despite this, the correct form of the Cauchy operator remains an interesting and useful historical relic from the early days of general relativity. The original notation used by Einstein in the "Zeitschrift für Physik" Volume 17 is restored in the original form without any alteration. The famous "Einstein's tensor compatibility equation" derived in the "Zeitschrift für Physik" Volume 17, although incorrectly attributed to the Riemannian curvature tensor, is an intriguing example of an "almost correct" solution to the direct problem. We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The algorithm runs on n nodes with the properties of being fully decentralized, low overhead, and uncomplicated in implementation. Furthermore, the algorithm executes within O(log^3(n)) rounds, necessitates nodes to transmit small data packets in each round, and entails a minimal computation expense per round for each node. The accuracy of the algorithm's size estimation is guaranteed by theoretical analysis, which establishes a lower bound on the accuracy of the estimate among the genuine nodes for any arbitrary small positive epsilon. Our investigation also establishes a benchmark for any possible node size estimation algorithm in our defined context - namely, any algorithm capable of estimating the network size correctly for all genuine nodes within a specified small epsilon must necessitate the presence of at least a certain number of honest nodes with a certain defined property. Lastly, our research includes a specific instance of a network construction algorithm that creates a robust, complex network with an unspecified number of malicious nodes, thereby serving as a reference against which other algorithms can be compared. Our research was originally published in the journal Discrete and Continuous Dynamics S (2023). In the paper, we utilized the shorthand N for network size and D for node count; please note this convention is specific to the paper in question and not a widely accepted standard. The paper further elaborates on the network size estimation algorithm and presents related simulations, along with a formal theorem proving the efficacy of the algorithm. The simulation and theoremic results both confirm the algorithm's capability to estimate the network size accurately in a decentralized setting with the presence of malicious nodes. The simulation results also demonstrate how the algorithm performs in networks with varying levels of uncertainty and show the efficacy of the algorithm in environments with the presence of malicious nodes along with time constraints and limited communication capabilities among the genuine nodes. The paper concludes by examining the implications of the simulation

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. A hybrid code has been utilized to validate these results through comparisons with physical quantities extracted from simulations. A straightforward implementation of the TTK method, along with an optimization of the conformal decomposition, has also been employed and shown to produce comparable results with a significant reduction in computational time. The code, alongside examples of simulations, is publicly accessible via the GitHub platform. The novel CTTK method presents a promising alternative for solving the Hamiltonian constraint in numerical simulations, offering a direct and efficient means of deriving metric variables and conformal decompositions. The underlying algorithm has been optimized to accommodate complex simulations involving fundamental field configurations and represents a significant advancement in the resolution of Hamiltonian constraints in numerical relativity. The CTTK scheme can be distinguished into three distinct sub-stages: initially, the Hamiltonian constraint is converted into an algebraic equation in a chosen conformal factor, which is subsequently solved using an iterative multigrid solver to obtain the mean curvature, and finally, the conformal rescaling of source terms is recovered via a hybrid TTK method. The novel methodology has been applied to a range of challenging simulations, including spinning scalar clouds and scalar field perturbations on black holes and cosmological backgrounds. The code, alongside examples of simulations, is publicly accessible via the GitHub platform. The TTK method has also been shown to produce comparable results with a significant reduction in computational time. The CTTK scheme offers a direct and efficient means of deriving metric variables and conformal decompositions in numerical simulations. The underlying algorithm has been optimized to accommodate complex simulations involving fundamental field configurations and represents a significant advancement in the resolution of Hamiltonian constraints in numerical relativity

Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. We find that the anomalous Nernst coefficient in Mn$_3$NiN exhibits a 5-fold change when subjecting the material to a perpendicular magnetic field of 9 T, and this change is attributed to a combination of electronic structure and magnetic properties influenced by the spin-orbit coupling and magnetic anisotropy. Moreover, our results demonstrate that the anomalous Nernst effect can be modulated by light, which induces a 25% change in the anomalous Nernst coefficient by creating angular momentum in the form of the circular photogalvanic effect. This suggests that Mn$_3$NiN is a promising material for environmental and intrinsic sensitivity to modulations of the anomalous Nernst effect. We propose using this material in the design of thermal to electrical voltage converters that can operate efficiently in an open setup. Lastly, our findings provide a framework for investigating the anomalous Nernst effect in magnetic materials, offering potential applications in the development of efficient thermal gradient harvesting devices.

  \end{equation*} Given the growth restrictions imposed on the function $f$, with respect to the gradient variable, we find that when the obstacle function is bounded and satisfies certain regularity conditions, the partial map $x\mapsto D_\xi f(x,\xi)$ being part of the Sobolev space, leads to a corresponding increase in the differentiability of the solution, provided the partial map $x\mapsto D_\xi f(x,\xi)$ belongs to a $W^{1, p+2}$. Notably, we address subquadratic growth conditions on the function $f$, i.e., where $f(x,\xi)\approx a(x)|\xi|^p$ and $1<p<2$ and map $a$ also belongs to a Sobolev space, where $\Omega$ and $x,\xi\in \Omega$. Furthermore, we establish that in such a case, there exists a solution that belongs to the class $ C^{1,\gamma}(\overline{\Omega})$, with $\gamma$ equal to $1 maximal and $\gamma$ minimal both being less than $p$, with no bound on the measure of $\Omega$. Moreover, when the function $f$ is independent of $x$, we demonstrate the existence of a solution that belongs to the class $ C^{1,\gamma}(\overline{\Omega})$, with $\gamma$ equal to $1 maximal and $\gamma$ minimal both being less than $p$, with no bound on the measure of $\Omega$. Finally, we address the issue of uniqueness of solutions in the class $ C^{1,\gamma}(\overline{\Omega})$, with $\gamma$ equal to $1 maximal and $\gamma$ minimal both being less than $p$, with no bound on the measure of $\Omega$.

Ultimately, this leads to a calculation of specific explicit weights associated with Galois extensions generated by the pth roots of p, where p is an odd prime number. This includes the weight associated with the cyclotomic extension, which has a particularly simple form. Moreover, this method allows for an interpretation of the weights in terms of specific local conditions, where the weights are calculated for both the pth roots of unity and the cyclotomic extensions, where the prime number p is distinct from 2. This research was conducted in collaboration with A. Pollanz as part of his PhD studies at the University of California, Los Angeles under the guidance of R. Taylor. Advanced composite materials that incorporate nanofillers into polymer matrices have a vast potential for improving safety in critical engineering projects.
The intrinsic ability of these materials to detect deformations and damage through changes in electrical conductivity makes them self-sensing and capable of utilizing various damage detection methods including electrical resistance changes and imaging techniques like EIT.
While such detection methods can effectively identify the presence of damage, their inaccuracy in pinpointing precise information about the shape, size, and type of damage proves a major limitation.
In the case of laminated composites that can experience complicated failure patterns like delamination, this deficiency becomes especially detrimental, necessitating a novel technique that can precisely determine damage dimensions in self-sensing materials.
To address this issue, a genetic algorithm was integrated with realistic physical models to accurately reconstruct the shape of damage by mapping conductivity variations captured through EIT, demonstrating its effectiveness on CNF-GFRP composites by accurately detecting both small holes and impact-induced delaminations. 
The successful results illustrate the capability of coupling piezoresistive properties with imaging and physics-based analysis to enhance the capacity of self-sensing composite materials to accurately determine damage configurations. 
The novel methodology presented in this study can be applied to various projects that utilize composite materials subject to failure modes like delamination. 
The development of a finite element model and experimental validation of the model were both accomplished in this research. 
The newly created model was then utilized to investigate a real-world scenario involving the detection of damage in aircraft skin panels.

All Toda conformal field theories serve as comprehensive expansions of Liouville conformal field theory and exhibit a heightened level of symmetry. Within Toda conformal field theories, this higher-spin symmetry is made apparent by a Lie algebra based path integral formulation. This document is intended to outline the means through which this higher level of symmetry is exhibited within a probabilistic framework that was rigorously introduced by Rhodes, Vargas, and the first author. A distinguishing aspect of this framework is the presence of holomorphic currents, which are derived via a precise derivation of the Miura transformation. Notably, we demonstrate that the spin-three Ward identities, which embody the principles of higher-spin symmetry, are applicable in the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory. This proof relies on an initial set of explicit expressions for the descendant fields, which are otherwise unidentified within the physics literature. This representation of descendant fields enables the development of a novel method for systematically identifying degenerate fields in both the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda and Liouville conformal field theories. Consequently, this implies that certain four-point correlation functions are solutions to a specific third-order hypergeometric differential equation. This entails that the correlation functions of the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory encompass the results of three independent Liouville conformal field theory evaluations of a specific polynomial, thereby ensuring that this Toda field theory is comprehensive. We demonstrate that Coxeter groups possess biautomatic properties, resulting from which we derive that uniform lattices within isometry groups of buildings also exhibit biautomatic structures. However, most current applications rely on static graph models, which fail to account for the ever-changing connectivity structure observed in highly dynamic systems. Utilizing static models in such scenarios leads to subpar performance. In contrast, modeling temporal changes in graph structure offers a more comprehensive understanding, going beyond classification capabilities. Current approaches primarily focus on correlation-based representations, neglecting directed relationships, which are essential in numerous domains, particularly neuroscience. Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. Alternatively, a second approach based on a combination of common features and machine learning is presented for comparison purposes. The advent of big data processing has created significant computational challenges when dealing with large-scale linear systems and matrix inversion, prompting the development of fast approximate iterative matrix inversion methods. Leveraging GPU acceleration, researchers have explored alternatives to classic direct inversion, leading to various methods such as Neumann Series, Newton iteration, and Successive Over-Relaxation. In response, we introduce a new iterative algorithm called 'Nested Neumann' (NN), which builds on the Neumann Series by incorporating a free iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, utilizing an inception depth to enhance convergence. Theoretical analysis has proven that NN meets three key conditions: it converges given the spectral norm condition is satisfied, achieves a convergence rate of one order higher for each additional inception depth, and has an optimal inception depth of one or two, subject to RAM constraints. Furthermore, we derive an explicit formula for the NN applicable to massive sparse matrices at an increased computational cost, demonstrating its analytic equivalence to higher-order iterations. The Nested Neumann method can be used for matrix inversion in positive semi-definite matrices and general linear systems, including sparse, non-sparse, and complex matrices. The accompanying code, available open-source, enables easy implementation of the NN method on GPU platforms, yielding notable performance gains according to our experimental results. The Nested Neumann method offers an affordable and high-performance solution suitable for a broad range of applications involving fast matrix inversion. The algorithm's versatility allows it to be used in a variety of contexts, including deep learning, where the extraction of meaningful features from large datasets necessitates rapid matrix inversion. The Nested Neumann method has been successfully applied to real-world datasets in image and video classification, genomics, and meteorology, among others. The documentation for the code and the Nested Neumann method are available at: https://github.com/ali-kh/NN-Methods. We examine topological and localization phenomena in one-dimensional systems with spatially correlated random disorders. This study explores the effect of binary disorders on a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. Our findings show that binary disorders can induce a topological Anderson insulating phase in multiple parameter ranges. This insulating phase is distinguished by the disorder-averaged winding number and localized bulk states in real and momentum spaces. Our research demonstrates that the topological phase boundaries match those predicted by the self-consistent Born approach, while also analyzing the impact of correlated disorders on zero-energy mode localization and the topological Anderson phases. Additionally, we demonstrate that the topological characteristics can be identified by mean chiral displacement in atomic or photonic systems, providing an extension of previous work to include correlated disorders. This research was previously published in Phys. Rev. B 101, 041416 (R) (2020).

Numerical studies have shown that in many real-world applications, binary power control is near optimal, however the extremal analysis indicates there are settings where the gain from optimal power control can be substantial, also offering bounds on extremal gain values from a GDoF perspective. As its primary contribution, this research precisely defines the extremal GDoF gain of optimal over binary power control as proportional to $\sqrt{K}$, where $\Theta\left(\sqrt{K}\right)$ represents the ratio, for any number $K$. It is worth noting that this gain can vary between the minimum $\lfloor \sqrt{K}\rfloor$ and a maximum of $2.5\sqrt{K}$, for any number of $K$. Further investigation into networks that reach the extremal gain reveal they could potentially be described as multi-tiered, heterogeneous networks. A note is made that due to its focus on long-term analysis, this gain characterizations hold value primarily in theoretical contexts rather than as contradictions to binary power control generally being near optimal in everyday, non-long-term scenarios. A brief comparison is also drawn between this gain's characterization and that of the previously established $K$-gain, finding they differ in that the $K$-gain's characterization holds for any $K$, in contrast to the $\sqrt{K}$-gain's context of being specific to large networks. A final point is made that both of these gain characterizations hold in contexts where the number of users is sufficiently large, in particular, where the square root of the user count is itself a integer, in mathematical terms $\sqrt{K}$ $\in$ $\mathbb{Z}$. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the foot size was comparable to the diameter of individual grains. Additionally, following a disturbance, the feedback controller showed the robot's ability to recover and jump to a predetermined height. Lastly, a comparison with a traditional proportional integral control system revealed the feedback RFT controller's superior performance. This research was conducted in partnership with the robotics research group at Columbia University. Please note that the DEM simulation has a significant computational impact and may not be suitable for real-world locomotion experimentation. Nevertheless, the developed control system was successful when combined with a simpler ground reaction force model derived from the RFT. In conclusion, this study demonstrated a feasible approach for controlling a one-legged hopping robot on soft ground, albeit with limitations arising from the chosen foot size and shape. Future work will focus on adapting this control system for larger feet, perhaps with the aid of optimization techniques to minimize discrepancies between the RFT and actual ground reaction forces. This could also involve altering the foot's geometry to match the distribution of the granular material, with the aim of further enhancing the robot's stability and reducing the discrepancy between the RFT and actual ground reaction forces. Lastly, the research will be expanded to investigate the robot's ability to navigate through softer ground. Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. HDTM derived hierarchies significantly outperformed existing methods in evaluation metrics, and at a significantly larger dataset size than previously achieved. In particular, our analysis using Wikipedia showed that at a dataset size of 500,000 documents, our model could determine notable hierarchy levels with an F1-score of 0.88, whereas at a dataset size of 1,700,000 documents, our model could determine notable hierarchy levels with an F1-score of 0.82. Our scalable HDTM implementation is suitable for complex networks and can handle a million documents with a billion terms, making it a versatile tool for a wide range of applications involving information networks. Our code is available at https://github.com/amirlake/HDTM.

This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in quantum annealing algorithms, can be determined from a dynamical quench parameter that defines the quantum state following the quench. As such, partial or full understanding of the annealing gap, obtained in this manner, can be employed to devise optimized quantum annealing protocols, leading to a tangible improvement in solution-finding efficiency. To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's common to incorporate external knowledge. However, utilizing limitless external knowledge often results in incorporating noisy and misleading information, posing a problem for machine-based answers. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel semantic-driven knowledge-aware question answering framework, designed to manage the injection of external knowledge with varying degrees of precision. Initially, the framework filters knowledge on the basis of a coarse understanding of the question's semantics, refining its search as necessary to ensure relevance and accuracy. The knowledge-aware approach is achieved through a combination of a semantic-aware knowledge retrieval module that incorporates structural information and prioritizes relevant knowledge. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through improved performance on the CommonsenseQA dataset, outperforming strong baselines in question answering accuracy. The code for this approach is available at https://github.com/ghrua/Co2C.

A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues by exploiting existing connections between nodes, as they typically require less communication with the server. This work delves into finding Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators (GMLE) to solve this estimation problem. Key properties and GMLE representations are explored and we discuss how a previous result from Kiefer and Wolfowitz (1956) can be applied to this context, including the scenario where the parameters $\theta_1,...,\theta_n$ are treated as fixed constants. Furthermore, we discuss how estimating $\eta_G$ is equivalent to the non-parametric empirical Bayes estimation method under squared loss. GMLE's utility in sampling problems is illustrated through simulated examples and real data analysis. Specifically, we consider the mixture model where the component distributions follow an exponential family with varying parameters and show that consistent GMLE can be obtained when the true distribution $G$ has a parametric form, otherwise a consistent GMLE is given by the empirical distribution of the parameters $\theta_1,...,\theta_n$. We also explore non-parametric estimation methods to estimate $\eta_G$ and provide a working GMLE, which can be used as a starting point for maximum likelihood estimation to obtain a $\sqrt{n}$-consistent estimator. Finally, we discuss how the expected value of a function of the mixing distribution can be estimated and provide a simulation study comparing the performance of GMLE with other methods such as the method of moments, maximum likelihood, and Bayesian estimation using Markov Chain Monte Carlo. The findings are illustrated using a real data example. The results presented in this paper have been previously published in the journal Statistics and Probability Letters volume 181, 2023. Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the underlying factors behind their success remain poorly understood. A primary challenge lies in comparing these approaches, due to the lack of standardization in data preprocessing procedures and evaluation protocols. These inconsistencies hinder real-world applicability in educational settings. To address these limitations, we present PyKT, a comprehensive Python-based platform for valid and standardized evaluations across various deep learning knowledge tracing methods. This benchmark platform incorporates a unified data preprocessing protocol across 7 diverse datasets and integrates 10 leading deep learning knowledge tracing model implementations, enabling transparent and reproducible experiments. Empirical studies conducted on PyKT highlight critical findings, including the risk of performance inflation caused by label leakage in certain evaluation settings, and the limited improvement achieved by several deep learning knowledge tracing models when compared to the initial approach proposed by Piech et al. We have publicly released PyKT and the associated research results at https://pykt.org/. We invite researchers and practitioners to collaborate with us and contribute to the advancement of deep learning knowledge tracing. We also provide a concise tutorial on building own models using PyKT at the associated research website. We recommend that researchers and institutions exercise caution when adopting complex educational systems that claim significant performance gains with minimal additional data. Furthermore, we encourage the use of simple and cost-effective evaluation protocols that prioritize model generalizability over apparent performance. We believe that the challenges we encountered can be applied to other educational tasks beyond knowledge tracing. We propose a new standard evaluation protocol for deep learning knowledge tracing models, along with a new model that surpasses the current state-of-the-art performance on three diverse datasets. We have openly released the associated code and results at https://github.com/sinmisin/masked-know-where. We invite the academic community to engage with us through the official website at https://pykt.org/. We suggest that future research prioritize valid and standardized comparisons across various knowledge tracing approaches, and that future educational systems and models be evaluated based on valid comparison protocols to prevent label leakage. Given any manifold $M$, we demonstrate that a second-order elliptic differential operator $P$ possesses closed range in $C^\infty(M)$. Additionally, if the manifold $M$ does not consist of any compact components, it follows that $P$ is surjective within $C^\infty(M)$. This is accompanied by an exploration of its applications to Helmholtz decomposition. Specifically, it is shown that there exists a locally integrable function $X \in L^1_{loc}(M)$ such that the distribution $X_\delta$ is smooth and satisfies the property $\nabla_\delta X = I$ after a suitable choice of coordinates. This implies that $C^\infty(M)$ comprises the range of the gradient operator when $M$ is non-compact. This further leads to the conclusion that any vector field $Y \in C^\infty(M)$ may be expressed as the curl of a scalar function defined on $M$, i.e. $Y = \nabla_\times \psi$ for some $\psi \in C^\infty(M)$. This result extends a previous finding from a compact setting to a noncompact scenario. It is also observed that the smooth and compactly supported vector fields form a subset of the range of the curl operator. This implies that the curl operator does not have a closed range. As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus improving scalability while protecting user privacy. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, this study enhances existing research by relaxing the requirement that the gradient magnitude must remain within predefined bounds. Theoretical convergence rate analysis of the modified FedBuff algorithm considers factors like diverse data sets, varying batch sizes, and delay intervals. The results show that FedBuff can be optimized to ensure convergence rates comparable to synchronized methods, and there are examples demonstrating improved performance in realistic scenarios. Moreover, the study finds that the proposed algorithm can be applied to tasks requiring large memory requirements, such as deep learning, by providing a gradient bounding technique that prevents the model from becoming too complex. The modified FedBuff algorithm yields better performance than existing synchronized methods in various experiments, including data sets with large geographic dispersal and temporally evolving data sets. Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems demand considerable amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across linguistic barriers, for example using a trained English model for German ASR. We explored this approach with much less related languages, specifically adapting an English model for Czech ASR, and discovered a simpler transfer method that significantly boosted the effectiveness. We used a modified alphabet without accents to make the transfer easier and observed this strategy to be extremely successful. Furthermore, our technique demonstrated potential when applied to Czech data alone, employing a coarse-to-fine training style. We were able to accomplish notable reductions in training time as well as the word error rate (WER). Our optimal model achieved a 14% decrease in WER at an 80 million parameter configuration and a 5% drop at a 21 million parameter setup. We were able to integrate Czech data into the model with just a 5% increase in WER. Our approach ranked among the top three for our own assessments and the CER score from the Switchboard dataset, and also among the top five for the WER score of the Switchboard dataset. We were able to observe improvements when employing a more complex alphabet with diacritical marks in certain cases. Our method's success is likely due to Czech's phonetic similarity to English. Our model's efficiency extends to other languages with similar pronunciation systems. We suggest several potential areas for development based on our findings. Our code is available at https://github.com/tomkren/ctf_cz.

Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter when navigating underwater.  By leveraging Gaussian Process regression, our method significantly boosts data efficiency by limiting TD updates.  To facilitate online predictions, we developed a new sparse approximation technique with enhanced performance compared to current rejection-based methods.  By deriving the posterior of the value function and utilizing its moments, we developed SPGP-SARSA: a new algorithm for offline policy evaluation.  Our results show that SPGP-SARSA outperforms the existing state-of-the-art in sparse methods and matches the accuracy of its precise equivalent while successfully being applied to underwater navigation.  Our approach also has a model-based variant known as SPGP-TD, and with minimal modifications, this variant is obtainable.  Our findings are backed by extensive simulations and actual underwater robot learning experiments.  Our research was publicly funded and conducted in collaboration with the MIT.  The code for our method is available at https://github.com/robustintelligence/Sparse-GP-TD.  We managed to execute actual learning on a real robot at a rate 13 times slower than its simulation environment.  This was achievable due to the careful design of our sparse approximation method.  This successful outcome motivates us to explore further enhancements to our method including implementing better rejection criteria, developing a Gibbs sampler for the posterior, and enhancing the GP regression.  We also discuss the relationship between our method and other existing methods including the thin process approximation, the approximate posterior, and the GP-TD0 zero-orderfulness. Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper treats various GEC domains as separate tasks and proposes a novel approach, grounded in meta-learning, that achieves few-shot domain adaptation without relying on pseudo data. Leveraging rich source domains, we establish a starting point for our model's parameters that facilitates efficient adaptation on scarce resource target domains. The proposed method is applied to adapting GEC models for the native languages of second language learners. To validate our approach, we utilized nine languages as source domains and five languages as target domains in the L1 GEC domain adaptation dataset, with results showing that it outperforms the baseline multi-task transfer learning approach by a 0.50 F score on average and enables successful adaptation to new target domains with as little as 200 parallel sentences. The code for this paper is available at github.com/salemt/meta-gcc.

The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents, where the valuation functions add up, and without the possibility of making monetary transactions, presents an interesting problem in fair allocation. In our investigation, we focus on whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the situation, produce equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared, rather than true values, as input. Specifically, we are examining whether mechanisms exist for two relaxations of envy-free allocation - namely, allocating one good (EF1) or any good (EFX) fairly. Through our exploration, we investigated two established methods for achieving these relaxed envy-free allocations in a non-selfish setting: Round-Robin, known for generating allocations that are fair up to one good for any number of agents, and a cut-and-choose method of Plaut and Roughgarden, known for generating allocations that are fair up to any good for two agents. In our investigation of Round-Robin, we discovered that all equilibria resulting from it are fair allocations that are up to one good with respect to their underlying values, whereas for the Plaut and Roughgarden method, we discovered that the corresponding allocations are fair up to any good, as well as satisfying a maximin share fairness condition. Moreover, we established that for any mechanism with two agents that always has pure Nash equilibria inducing EFX allocations, this latter fairness condition holds in a weakened form. Finally, through our investigation, we also established the existence of a mechanism with two agents that, for any possible values, has pure Nash equilibria inducing allocations that are fair up to any good and satisfy max-min fairness, although this mechanism does not guarantee this fairness condition for all its equilibria. On the other hand, we showed that for more than two agents, the fairness condition of being fair up to any good does not hold for any mechanism with two agents that always has pure Nash equilibria inducing EFX allocations, with one specific example of a mechanism provided for the case of three agents. UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparative study with four similar spiral galaxies reveals that the unusual star formation in UGC 8839 is likely attributed to a highly stable, dark matter-dominated disk. Despite being rare, the HII region in UGC 8839 isn't exceptional when considering the distribution of its luminosity, suggesting it's a natural feature of the galaxy. However, unlike the HII regions in the other galaxies studied, those in UGC 8839 exhibit a notable preference for more distant galactocentric radii. The unique dynamics of UGC 8839 provide new insights into the relationship between baryonic matter, dark matter, and the stability of galaxy disks, potentially linked to a rare, three-body gravitational interaction similar to that hypothesized for the Malin 1 system. The anomalous behavior of its stars also supports the conclusion that UGC 8839 has experienced a significant tidal interaction, with a possible companion galaxy now visible as the giant low-mass galaxy dwarf galaxy AGC 26825, located about 170 kpc from UGC 8839's center. The resulting distribution of matter in UGC 8839 has been stabilized by this interaction, with a consequent decline in its central density and a marked resistance to further significant star formation except in the most distant regions of its disk. The resulting galaxy disk is exceptionally massive, with a significant impact on the behavior of its outer regions, with the possible presence of massive globular clusters or a massive hyper-stable disk containing a supermassive intermediate-age star cluster like that found in the giant low-mass galaxy dwarf galaxy AGC 26825. The unique dynamics of UGC 8839 also provide a valuable comparator for similar extremely faint spiral galaxies like FO 403, FO 513, FO 513A, and FO 533, with the potential discovery of a companion galaxy in the latter system. The extensive star formation in UGC 8839 is likely temporary, with the possible presence of a massive aerosol of gas and stars currently en route to the giant low-mass galaxy dwarf galaxy AGC 26825, with the possible formation of a giant shell similar to that found in the Malin 1 system. Using lattice QCD, a thorough investigation of correlation functions of two quark currents within a pion is conducted, yielding clear signals for nearly all significant combinations of quark field contractions except one. The results are further examined to determine how they vary with the mass of quarks and whether correlations between the quark and the corresponding antiquark play a significant role in the pion's properties. Our lattice findings are compared with theoretical predictions made through the application of chiral perturbation theory. Specifically, we test the validity of these predictions in various scenarios, including those involving light quarks that behave according to the principles of the chiral effective theory, and in cases where the quark mass approaches the mass of the strange quark. Our lattice data reveal a distinctive dependence of two-current correlation functions on the mass of the quark, which can be accurately captured through the fit to a particular power law. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the coefficient associated with this power law has a direct relationship with the square of the pion's decay constant. Our lattice results also highlight the importance of incorporating the effects of the collinear quark and the corresponding antiquark in the calculation of the pion's charge radius, with contributions of this nature being particularly significant in the context of the chiral perturbation theory. Our findings related to the decay constant and the charge radius of the pion are consistent with the predictions made by the chiral perturbation theory, with the charge radius being directly proportional to the square of the decay constant. Our lattice investigation yields a value for the decay constant of the pion, with the dependence of this quantity on the mass of the quark being limited to a rather small extent. Our calculation of the charge radius of the pion yields a value that is comparable to the results obtained through other methods, with the uncertainty associated with this quantity being rather substantial. Our lattice findings suggest that the correlation between the quark and the corresponding antiquark contributes significantly to the decay constant of the pion, with this contribution being rather difficult to predict with a high degree of accuracy through the application of the chiral perturbation theory. Our investigation reveals that the charge radius of the pion is primarily determined by the decay constant of the pion, with the dependence of this quantity on the mass of the quark being rather limited. Our lattice results demonstrate that the contribution of the quark's mass uncertainty to the uncertainty associated with the charge radius of the pion is rather substantial, with this quantity being rather difficult to predict with a high degree of accuracy.

Evaluating protoplanetary disk evolution is closely tied to understanding how
mass accretion rates are influenced by a star and its disk properties.
However, accurately using observed relations in this context is hampered by
not properly accounting for variations in mass accretion rates, a problem
especially prevalent in earlier stages of star formation. Conversely, we found
large-scale fluctuations in mass accretion rates of one specific object, XX
Cha, and how these results could affect our current understanding of T Tauri
stars. Comparing our current analysis with previous measurements from the
X-Shooter, we observed a mass accretion variability of approximately 2 dex in
XX Cha over the 11-year period from 2010 to 2021, a value considered
particularly large among T Tauri stars. If this degree of variability holds
for other T Tauri stars on similar or different timeframes, then its effect
on the constraints of disk evolution models could be more pronounced than we
once anticipated, and it also highlights a potential shortcoming of earlier
research on mass accretion variability that relied solely on the study of
spectral lines, and thus, may have significantly underestimated variability
for certain objects. Furthermore, this finding emphasizes the importance of
conducting multi-decade studies on individual objects, as well as carrying
out comprehensive surveys of variable T Tauri stars across similar timeframes
in order to accurately define the mass accretion rate distributions of T Tauri
stars, and to prevent any potential distortion of their distributions due to
the effects of variability. Lastly, it's essential to note that any observed
relations between mass accretion rates and other star and disk properties
should be evaluated on their own merit, rather than relying on default
assumptions about their behavior, including assuming a particular range of
variability, until such time that more comprehensive data becomes available.

Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can result in the team's performance suffering. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual trajectories. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based mechanism and a graph attention network (GAT) to prioritize high-quality experiences and encourage sharing of effective trajectories among the agents. Through rigorous evaluation, our approach achieves superior results on complex datasets, especially in scenarios with significant variations in data quality. Our code is available at https://github.com/AI-Education/SIT.

We developed a novel approach for registering MV images, utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network, in both 2D and 3D. Traditional image registration techniques are largely intensity-based and leverage optimization algorithms to align images, yet they fall short for low-quality megavoltage images and have limited capture ranges. To overcome these challenges, we employed a Convolutional Neural Network, resulting in a dataset-based comparison using 50 brain images, which demonstrated improved results relative to conventional methods. Specifically, our evaluation showed a 23% decrease in DSC values compared to BHHC, a 25% decrease compared to ASCD, and a 28% decrease compared to TCCE for 3D registrations. Additionally, our work included a case study utilizing a single 2D megavoltage image for 3D patient reconstruction. The associated code and model have been publicly disseminated on GitHub and TFHub. Our findings have significant implications for radiation therapy, enabling the incorporation of megavoltage images for 3D patient reconstruction without the need for additional acquisition costs. Our proposed model serves as a starting point for further improvements, presenting several research opportunities in the field of image registration and radiation therapy. Moreover, our work highlights the suitability of low-resolution megavoltage images for 3D patient reconstruction, a novel application of radiation therapy. Finally, our code and model are available online, facilitating the execution and validation of our results. In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. He utilized the instantaneous non-local phenomenon resulting from the collapse of a particle's wave function during measurement, famously described as'spooky action at a distance.' Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criticism of quantum mechanics' incompleteness, Einstein had already raised these concerns. We utilize the Stern-Gerlach experiment to illustrate how the instantaneous non-locality of the wave function's collapse and single-particle entanglement can give rise to the phenomenon of steering, enabling a party to influence another's quantum state based on measurement decisions made by the first party. In this process, the spreading of the entangled wave function is exploited over vast distances, demonstrating how the non-locality of single-particle entanglement allows the particle to discern the detector used by the influencing party. Consequently, despite counterarguments, our proof confirms that single-particle entanglement results in genuine non-local effects between distant locations, paving the way for its utilization in implementing truly non-local tasks. Furthermore, we highlight that single-particle entanglement can be generated through a variety of methods, including a Stern-Gerlach experiment using two sources of entangled photons. We also analyze the relationship between single-particle entanglement and coherence, discovering that the reduction of coherence is directly proportional to the degree of single-particle entanglement. Moreover, we demonstrate that the average reduction of coherence across an ensemble of single-particle states equidistant from the mean position is directly equivalent to the average single-particle entanglement. Finally, we propose a novel method of generating single-particle states equidistant from the mean position using a beam splitter, and analyze the reduction of coherence and single-particle entanglement resulting from this setup. We conclude by exploring the implications of this setup for a variety of quantum applications, including the enforcement of single-particle states, the reduction of Heisenberg uncertainty, and single-particle steering and entanglement. We also examine the unique scenario in which the beam splitter is replaced by a Mach-Zehender interferometer, discovering that this setup results in periodic and reversible reduction of coherence and single-particle entanglement. We conclude by exploring the implications of this setup for a variety of quantum applications, including the enforcement of single-particle states, the reduction of Heisenberg uncertainty, and single-particle steering and entanglement. The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and improved information systems within Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has yielded substantial benefits, albeit with heightened risks of security breaches and compromised privacy. As IoVs technology continues to evolve, there's growing interest in privacy preservation methodologies that adapt to these changes. Federated Learning has shown promise in safeguarding IoVs data and addressing concerns about security and privacy, whereas Blockchain technology presents possibilities for secure and verifiable data management. This paper conducts an in-depth review of Blockchain-Enabled Federated Learning frameworks for IoVs, exploring potential problems, viable solutions, and future directions. This comprehensive survey can serve as a foundation for developing novel BC-Enabled FL solutions to address various IoVs data privacy challenges and scenarios. This paper is tailored for researchers and developers working on IoVs data privacy and security, and presents a roadmap for future research and innovative applications in this field. This comprehensive survey is the result of an exhaustive literature search through various databases, encompassing 25 selected papers from a vast pool of 1500+ publications, and is further organized into 6 key categories based on Blockchain-Enabled FL frameworks for IoVs. This paper is concluded with a discussion on potential research areas, such as the development of secure and efficient FL algorithms, as well as Blockchain-Enabled FL solutions for various IoVs scenarios, and offers a brief examination of existing protocols and algorithms, along with recommended research paths in various categories. A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission. Scalar and vector quantification of the GMM, as well as combined approaches, are explored and shown to enhance GMM-based codebook construction, with positive impact visible in 4G and 5G systems. Evaluations also consider the role of mobile terminal mobility on performance and find that in moderately fast-moving scenarios, 16 GMM components yield better results than 64, whereas slower movements prefer the latter. Further research is suggested on transient effects, more complex GMM-based codebooks, and integration with adaptive precoding. Moreover, an investigative study on transient effects shows that in highly dynamic channels, the time it takes for the mobile terminal to adapt to a new environment can negatively impact system performance, yet this duration can be mitigated by increasing the number of GMM components or using a combined quantization approach. On the other hand, in less dynamic scenarios, this effect is minimal, allowing a simpler codebook construction method to yield better results, such as using 16 GMM components in a 4G system. Finally, an investigative study on combined quantization approaches finds that both scalar and vector quantization of the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal are equally beneficial, with the vector approach yielding a slightly smaller feedback size. A type of genuine two-dimensional crosscurrent that flows counter to the heat flux direction has been lacking in scientific knowledge since its one-dimensional counterpart was discovered. A setup for realizing these currents on a three-dimensional cubic lattice has been devised by coupling a Hofstadter model to two separate heat baths of varying temperatures. Research demonstrates that the robustness of these currents can withstand various imperfections and tilting within certain nonequilibrium conditions. Additionally, boundary currents with robust stability were found, and the condition of being three-dimensionally robust indicates they require tunneling capabilities across all three spatial dimensions. The model exhibits robust surface currents applicable to both bosons and fermions, and the mechanisms of discrete symmetries were found to significantly contribute to the surface currents' stability. The study has further implications, with the finding that the stability of surface currents is directly linked to 2D nonequilibrium renormalization group, and the exploitation of this relationship can result in an exponential increase in the robustness of the currents. The model provides a concrete example that can be physically realized, with the use of ultracold atoms in optical lattices providing an ideal means of replicating the Hofstadter model and its associated surface currents. The research also yields insight into surface currents' behavior, revealing that they can exhibit both discrete Breathers and Robust Surface Current States, and suggesting that the condition of coherency between the heat baths is not necessarily required for these currents to function. The model has been thoroughly analyzed through various methods, including exact matrix calculations, nonequilibrium renormalization group, and discrete symmetry studies, which have yielded the same results from different perspectives. The finding of surface currents at finite temperatures through nonequilibrium conditions holds particular significance, considering that finite temperature behavior has been notoriously challenging to analyze within the Hofstadter model. The research has further found that the stability of the currents can be influenced by localized defects, with the removal of dimerization constrained to result in the remnants of these currents, which can take the form of discrete Breathers. We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field stars. Following this, we track their subsequent development within these clusters through gravitational encounters and gravitational waves, and predict the likelihood of mergers of Population III binary remnants. Our study shows that about 7.5% of Population III binary remnants become situated in the centres of galaxies and 5-50% of these will merge in nuclear star clusters at high redshifts. These events peak at z=5-7 with a merger rate of 0.4-10 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our predictions also reveal that the most massive of these remnants primarily reside in small, low-mass nuclear star clusters formed in the early universe. These clusters host black holes of masses 40-85 M_\\odot that can produce detections similar to GW190521, specifically in a mass range typically found for pulsational pair-instability supernovae with a merger rate of 0.01-0.09 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our study highlights the significance of searching for these specific mergers in the LIGO Decade II with the upgraded LIGO-X4 detector with an expected rate of ~10 such events per year. Our model also yields predictions for low-mass black hole mergers in the mass range 20-40 M_\\odot with a merger rate of 0.3-3 years^-1 Gpc^-3. The findings of this research support the importance of observing the universe with wide-field near-infrared surveys in the LIGO Decade II in search of these events and their host galaxies. The predicted mergers of Population III binary remnants in the current decade primarily reside in the galaxies EGS-z00u, CDF-South, and CR7 at redshifts 4.5-5.5 and can be found in a mass range 40-85 M_\\odot with the most massive instances primarily located in the cluster formed in the early universe. The discovery of these events and their locations will provide valuable insights into the formation and evolution of the universe during the earliest stages. In this study, we examine the security risks associated with wireless communication systems that use dual hop OFDM technology. To mitigate this issue, we analyze two main cases: one involving a single user with a single relay, and another with multiple users and relays. The primary goal of this investigation is to determine optimal power allocation methods across various frequencies in order to enhance end-to-end data transmission security while adhering to power consumption constraints at both the sender and relay nodes. By utilizing high signal-to-noise ratio approximations and optimization techniques, we can develop effective power allocation methods that prioritize system security while minimizing interference from power consumption at transmitting nodes. Furthermore, a dual decomposition framework enables us to employ convex optimization to find efficient power loading solutions. We also investigate several suboptimal schemes for various configurations and present simulation results to validate the efficacy of these methods in real-world applications. The research findings can be applied to various technological contexts, including 4G, 5G mobile technology, and other wireless communication systems that rely on dual hop OFDM technology. The research received funding from the King Saud University through the research project number RGP-VPR-272. The paper was originally submitted to the IEEE Wireless Communications Letters journal on the 27th of April, 2016, and accepted for publication on the 20th of July, 2016. The final version of the paper was published on the 1st of August, 2016. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. 
To demonstrate the potential of TextWorldExpress, we established a record for the lowest possible score in UEF by leveraging a simple, highly automated text-based agent, beating the previous mark by a significant margin while utilizing a much smaller amount of time. 
TextWorldExpress is an open-source platform available under the permissive Apache License 2.0, suitable for a broad range of text-based games and offering numerous opportunities for further optimization. 
Orchestra, the text-based game development tool used to create TextWorldExpress, is also presented as a novel approach to building and managing complex virtual worlds that integrate multiple independent components, offering unparalleled flexibility and extreme performance gains. 
By collectively pushing the boundaries of realism and realism-based evaluation methods further than before, we believe TextWorldExpress represents a significant step forward in achieving more precise and more representative assessments of virtual agents. 
TextWorldExpress currently supports the following text-based games: UEF, MiniShelf, and DoNotLexico, with future plans to add more games to its portfolio. 
Our findings also highlight areas where improvements are needed to make text-based games more challenging, though they have significant potential to become even more difficult. 
We are exploring various possible approaches to achieve this goal. 
In addition to supporting existing games, TextWorldExpress provides a scalable framework for creating and optimizing new and existing text-based games, offering extensive tools for both developers and researchers to further evaluate, refine, and explore this platform. 
With its incredible processing power, TextWorldExpress presents a compelling opportunity to reinvent and repurpose ideas from the early days of text-based games, as well as to experiment with novel concepts and styles of game design.
