In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios. Our results demonstrate that separating tasks with modular networks
can prevent performance degradation and achieve high success rates in complex
situations. Moreover, we observe no increase in data collection costs during
learning. Our code is available at: https://github.com/ghul5/MultiTaskDynamicsLearning.

We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques. By integrating these results, we derive several notable consequences, including a more robust form of the Godel Incompleteness Theorem, as well as an Undefinability Theorem for truth, both of which have been previously established through other methods. Additionally, we examine the implication of combining these results within a specific formal system, revealing that such a system is capable of expressing the concept of definability, which in turn implies the automatic proof of its own incompleteness, as well as the undecidability of questions pertaining to the validity of its own formulas. Furthermore, we derive an expression that can be used to demonstrate the undecidability of any theory that contains this specific formal system, and finally, we conclude by discussing the limited scope of these results, which are restricted to the domain of first-order logic and cannot be extended to more versatile systems that are capable of describing the concept of itself. Nonetheless, within this confined context, these combined theorems hold an significant and enduring value, as they have been consistently utilized in numerous celebrated proofs of mathematical undecidability.

In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space. By applying transformation techniques, this extension is shown to enable the three balls theorem to be formulated for eigenfunctions of the Dirac operator. Additionally, this analysis leads to the discovery of a related inequality for the norm of these eigenfunctions. Furthermore, this result can be viewed as a specialized version of a broader three balls theorem established by the first author, which targets the R^n space. As such, this version provides an alternative proof of the space's three balls theorem. Moreover, this research introduces a new approach for demonstrating the boundedness of specific integral operators, which are composed of the Dirac operator and a gauge, using norms based on the space of hyperanalytic functions. This approach is shown to be effective in demonstrating the operator's continuity and, in specific cases, its boundedness, which in turn leads to the application of three balls theorem to these operators. In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image inpainting. By incorporating noise as input to the conditional GAN, we significantly enhanced the quality of sampled images and reduced the gap between generated and genuine images, as shown in experiments. The code for this project is available at https://github.com/shimothy/regularized Conditional WGAN.

This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds. Throughout this discussion, we emphasize the crucial role that symmetry plays in dynamical systems and the numerous applications of symmetric systems, such as circular cylinders in three-dimensional spaces. We also outline the methods for identifying symmetries in discrete-time systems and provide a clear distinction between the concepts of symmetry and cyclicality. We conclude by exploring the relationship between cyclicality and the existence of limit cycles in discrete-time systems and offer an example of a discrete-time system with a circular invariant manifold that exhibits multiple limit cycles. We also offer a solution to the problem of finding the largest circular invariant subset in a discrete-time system and provide computational instructions for implementing this solution. Finally, we outline potential future research directions related to the stability analysis of discrete-time systems. We hope that this article will serve as a valuable resource for both seasoned researchers and graduate students interested in the stability analysis of dynamical systems. The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. Furthermore, calculations determine the distance to this screen as well as the dimensions of the screen and the void, revealing that the screen encompasses a volume equivalent to multiple scattering screens seen in pulsar scintillation, offering an independent confirmation of the characteristics of the Local Bubble based solely on observations of a single pulsar over a prolonged period. This discovery highlights the capabilities of long-term pulsar monitoring in detailing the properties of the line-of-sight screens and the complex structure of the Local Bubble. This research was conducted using data from the Arecibo Ionization Disk Array, a facility that previously existed. This paper is based on a thesis titled: Probing the local interstellar medium with scintillometry of the bright pulsar B1133+16, submitted to the Leiden University Faculty of Mathematics and Natural Sciences in partial fulfillment of the requirements for the degree of Doctor of Philosophy. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis. Code for QPNet is available at: https://github.com/Parandosean/QPNet.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence. Additionally, this framework is utilized to recast and generalize results on the properties of shadows, specifically establishing connections to functors that are naturally marked and displaying how functors that are naturally marked can be constructed from shadows. These developments also enable the inclusion of Picard groupoids within the theory of shadows, allowing them to be viewed as a specific type of functors that are naturally marked. Lastly, this study demonstrates that functors that are naturally marked are essentially equivalent to functors that record information about the shadows of a bicategory, ultimately leading to the conclusion that functors that are naturally marked are, in fact, traces of that bicategory. This finding further supports the practical utility of functors that are naturally marked by highlighting how they can be applied to obtain results on the shadows of a bicategory, specifically the enlargement of shadows and the behavior of shadows under functors. Ultimately, this research on functors that are naturally marked also facilitates the introduction of a new operator, dubbed the trace operator, which acts on functors that are naturally marked, assigning to each natural transformation a shadow that is invariant under equivalence. This operator is foundational to the theory of functors that are naturally marked and provides a direct link to the properties of shadows, specifically the behavior of shadows under functors and the enlargement of shadows. Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Moreover, we introduce a new dataset called VGG-Sound Source, a comprehensive set of annotated video clips featuring sound sources with explicit bounding box markings. VGG-Sound Source surpasses existing datasets in scale, size, and category diversity, consisting of 5,000 videos spanning over 200 categories. Notably, it differs from Flickr SoundNet in that it is based on video data. Our algorithm also demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on this new dataset when compared to several baseline methods. Our code is available for public use at https://github.com/zwang-leehkg/SoundSourceLocalizaton.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion. LGCN's simplicity and efficiency make it suitable for a wide range of applications, from recommender systems to molecular graph representations. The code for LGCN is available at https://github.com/JinHePro/LGCN.

This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate. This inverse problem is ill-posed, and therefore, we develop a quasi-optimality cost functional to tackle it, yielding the existence of a minimizer for the cost functional, which in turn gives the source term with the desired stability properties. This source term is found by solving the structural acoustic FEniCs system, and we outline a numerical method to achieve this. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach and show that it can handle noisy data. This study extends previous inverse problems research by dealing with a more complex structural acoustic interaction model. Additionally, we offer a more practical and easier-to-implement solution strategy. Moreover, we provide a detailed discussion on the model's limitations and possible extensions, as well as a concise overview of the inverse problem mathematical framework. Lastly, we include a relevant numerical experiment involving a beam structure.

For a class of quadratic Hamiltonians, a transformation of Weyl-Wigner symbols through a change of variables reveals the canonical thermal equilibrium quantum states, using the Weyl-Wigner representations and metaplectic operators, whose associated unitary classical structures behave predictably under the transformation, exposing the complex symplectic matrix that dictates the entire thermal equilibrium state and thereby determines its thermal properties. Additionally, a thorough examination is performed of four distinct types of Hamiltonian dynamics: parabolic, elliptic, hyperbolic, and loxodromic dynamics. Semiclassical and high-temperature approximations are both determined and contrasted to their respective classical or quadratic behaviors. Moreover, a direct representation of the Metaplectic operator $\Gamma_\Omega$ is derived, demonstrating that $\Gamma_\Omega$ acts as a composition operator on the Weyl-Wigner symbols, and this action defines a classical Lie algebra structure that is directly linked to the complex classical Hamiltonian $\Omega$. Lastly, this framework is specifically applied to a harmonic oscillator, Reeb vector field, or more generally, a geodesic vector field on a complex manifold, resulting in a comprehensive understanding of its associated KMS states.

Additionally, this approach may provide a richer learning experience compared to traditional, purely analytical explanations. By directly comparing with $t_{2g}$ only or $e_g$ only models based on electron filling, we investigate the magnetic properties of all possible $d$-shell configurations, incorporating calculations of the total magnetic moment, orbital occupation, and effective spin-orbit coupling. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays. Our research was showcased at the Medical Imaging meets NeurIPS Workshop 2020, a satellite event of the 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems held in Vancouver, Canada. Our dataset and algorithm are available for public use at https://github.com/alexbdean/DiseaseAwareImageEditing. Our findings have been published in an abstract format in the Medical Imaging meets NeurIPS Workshop 2020 proceedings. ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and
advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include
numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool
encompasses several statistical techniques such as weighted PCA, elastic maps,
linear discriminant analysis, and decision tree construction, in addition to
K-Means clustering and multilinear regression. With customizable visualizations
and an interactive 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables the creation of 3D scenes
from data and facilitates rapid, in-depth analysis of data, encompassing
elementary to complex methodologies. The application is suited for individual
use and small teams, offering a user-friendly interface that simplifies
multidimensional data analysis and visualization. The source code of ViDaExpert
is publicly available on GitHub, under the terms of the BSD license. The
application as well as the source code can be downloaded from the project
website. The development of ViDaExpert was funded by the INRA, and the tool
has been utilized in various biological studies. The application can be used
from within a web browser, without the need for installation, at the address
http://vidaexpert.loria.fr/. The name of the application is derived from the
combination of the terms visualization, analysis, decision, and expertise. The
development of ViDaExpert was motivated by the limited interactivity of
custom-made data analysis tools and the high costs associated with the
development and deployment of Java-based applications. The application allows
